title: Failed-Part Bounty for Insurance Subrogation
one_liner: Pay plumbers a bounty to bag, photograph and chain-of-custody the pipe, supply line or fitting that failed, then sell the evidence and a brand-level failure database to insurers' subrogation units and manufacturers.
customer: Subrogation departments and subro vendors at regional and mutual homeowners insurers (the ones too small to send a forensic engineer to a $9k supply-line loss). Second buyers: plumbing manufacturers, distributors and private-label buyers who license the failure data.
problem: Water damage is among the top two homeowner claim categories. Product-defect subrogation (a supply line, PEX fitting, toilet connector, ice-maker line or water heater that failed early) only works if someone kept the failed part. The plumber is on scene 1 to 3 days before the adjuster, cuts the failed piece out, and tosses it in the truck-bed scrap bin. When the adjuster arrives the evidence is gone, the insurer eats the loss, and the manufacturer's lawyers cite spoliation. Insurers only hire the $2,000 forensic engineer on the big losses, so the routine $8-15k losses are never pursued. Meanwhile every plumber knows which brands are failing (certain plastic-nut braided lines, certain fill valves, certain fitting lots) but nobody aggregates it.
solution: A 90-second protocol and kit. Tamper-evident bag with a QR label, a phone flow (photo of the part in place, photo after removal, the manufacturer stamp or date code, homeowner e-signature by text, and the claim number if one exists). A weekly courier pickup from the shop and a climate-controlled evidence locker. Optional one-page factual cause-of-loss statement drawn from the same photos (sudden burst versus long-term seepage, which is exactly the 'gradual leak' exclusion that decides whether homeowners get paid). Every part is logged by brand, model, date code and failure mode, which builds a Backblaze-style public failure-rate report by product line. Insurers get the part plus a ready evidence package. The shop gets a bounty and a small line item on the invoice.
why_now: Water-loss severity has risen sharply and carriers are under pressure on homeowners loss ratios, so they are hunting for recovery dollars. Copper and steel tariffs plus the shift to PEX and imported fittings have flooded the market with cheaper components of unknown quality. Photo and OCR tooling now makes a cheap, standardized evidence workflow possible, and the subrogation trade press is openly saying evidence preservation is the make-or-break step.
revenue_model: Insurer or subro vendor pays $75-150 per part with a documented chain of custody, of which $40-60 goes to the shop and tech. Plus a 3-8% success share on any recovery that follows. Plus annual data licenses ($15-60k) to manufacturers, distributors and big-box private-label buyers, and per-report fees for expert-witness-ready packages.
non_obvious_insight: The evidence that decides tens of millions in recoveries is currently destroyed daily by the only people who touch it first, and the reason is not malice. Nobody pays a tech to spend 4 minutes and a bag on a piece of scrap. The plumber, not the adjuster, is the true first-notice-of-loss for the product itself. The bounty is a price signal, and the dataset that falls out is one nobody else can buy.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 shops through a local PHCC chapter and the owner Facebook and peer groups with a flat $50 per bag and a free kit. Design the label and the phone flow in a form tool. Collect the first 50 parts with photos. Take the first 20 case files to two regional mutual insurers and a subrogation vendor and ask them which they would have pursued. Sell a paid pilot for 100 parts on the strength of their answers.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Donan Engineering - Loss Logistics, Envista Forensics and Rimkus (forensic engineering / property loss consulting), LeakBot, ServiceTitan and CompanyCam (plumber field software). White space: Caveat: the session's WebSearch budget ran out (200 of 200) before any search ran. This verdict rests on direct page fetches of about a dozen vendor, industry and government sites, plus two empty GitHub searches. I did not check Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or trade press, so I could not rule out a small funded startup doing exactly this. Run 4-6 searches before committing money. Suggested queries: 'subrogation evidence preservation plumber', 'failed part bounty', 'water loss evidence kit', and the same on Crunchbase.

What I found is a real gap in what I could reach. Evidence logistics and forensic engineering exist for engineer-assigned losses (Donan, Envista, Rimkus). Insurer-funded plumber networks exist (LeakBot). Plumber field software exists (ServiceTitan, CompanyCam). No page I read describes any of these paying or equipping the plumber to retain the failed part on routine sub-$15k water losses. The public failure data I found is weak (SaferProducts.gov). Nothing I found is a date-code and brand-level failure-rate dataset.

Unserved specifically: (1) plumber-side capture at the moment of removal, including a per-part payment. (2) A neutral custodian and evidence package for the $8-15k tier, which is below the point where a $2k engineer is dispatched. (3) A structured brand, model and date-code failure dataset from real removed parts.

The main risks are structural, not competitive. (a) The plumber often arrives before a claim exists, so the claim number and the bounty payer are unknown at bagging. (b) Mitigation contractors and insurer-dispatched vendors may reach the site first on many losses. (c) The recovery economics of small product-defect claims are unproven, so insurers may not pay $75-150 for parts they would not pursue anyway. (d) A public brand-level failure report invites manufacturer legal pushback. (e) A 'cause-of-loss statement' from a tech risks unlicensed-engineering objections. (f) I could not fetch HomeServe (403), so I cannot say whether that plumber-network incumbent already does something like this.

title: Home Equity Assurance for Data Center Neighbors
one_liner: A neutral calculation agent runs a county-approved, developer-funded home-value guarantee for houses near proposed data centers, using pre-announcement baselines and public sale records with no sensors, and unspent escrow reverts to the developer, which makes it cheaper than $10k checks and more credible.
customer: Payer: independent data center developers and their CFOs and general counsel, especially those that have already tried lump-sum checks or buyouts and got 'bribe' coverage (NorthPoint-type offers, Mason County-type buyouts). Co-signer: county commissions that put the guarantee into a development agreement. Distribution partners: title and escrow companies, mortgage lenders and local realtors in the impact radius, who deliver claims at the point of sale. Beneficiaries: owner-occupants within roughly 1-3 miles.
problem: Residents' biggest fear is not a sensor reading, it is the value of their house. Developers are already spending on this fear in the worst way: NorthPoint's $10k-per-household offer ($45M across 4,500 households) was called a bribe, and Propmodo expects future offers to move to 'utility bill credits or property value guarantees rather than lump sums'. A check pays 100% of households for a risk that only touches the minority who sell at a loss, buys no trust, and leaves the price question unresolved. Home-value anecdotes are contested (a 4-bedroom listed 15-18% lower next to a Northern Virginia hyperscale site; the NAR 2026 Data Center Impact Report and local reporting disagree on how far effects reach), so both sides are arguing about a number nobody has pre-agreed.
solution: Product: a Property Value Assurance Program administered as a contract, not insurance. The developer is the obligor and funds an escrow (illustratively $3-5k per eligible household, against $10k of certain checks) with a corporate escrow agent at signing of the development agreement. We are the neutral calculation agent, the way a calculation agent works in a structured contract. Mechanics: (1) Freeze a reference value for each enrolled home at the date of first public disclosure of the project, using an AVM plus a broker price opinion (about $300), with a full appraisal only if disputed. (2) Publish a county-wide control index (repeat-sales or hedonic, plus matched control neighborhoods) so market moves are separated from project effects. (3) If the owner sells at arm's length within 10 years (listed 60+ days, arm's-length buyer), we pay from escrow the shortfall between the net sale price and the control-index-adjusted reference value, up to a cap (for example 20% of reference). (4) Unspent escrow reverts to the developer at year 10, or is split with a community fund. (5) No sensors: the trigger is a price versus a pre-agreed formula, so there is no argument about causation, only about arithmetic. Adverse selection and gaming are handled with the arm's-length rule, an exposure cap and a three-appraiser tie-break (already the norm in Mason County buyouts).
why_now: In 2026 lump-sum neighbor payments went mainstream and drew immediate backlash (NorthPoint, September 2026 coverage), while moratoria in NY (July 14) and Texas (Sept 21) plus local pauses give developers a reason to look for a structure that survives a hearing. Data-center adjacency is now a mainstream real-estate question: Realtor.com counts 108 ZIP codes with a large data center by June 2026, up from 12 in 2015, and NAR and HousingWire are publishing on it, so buyers and lenders already ask. AVMs, MLS and deed data are cheap and standardized. Wind developers have used property-value guarantees as permit conditions, so counties and lawyers recognize the form.
revenue_model: Paid by the developer from the program budget. Illustrative 3,000-household program: $300 per household enrollment (AVM, BPO, lien check, portal) = $900k; 1% per year of a $12M escrow = $120k; $1,500 per adjudicated sale claim; optional 50 bps share of escrow yield (T-bill yield on $12M is meaningful float for the agent-of-record bank to share). Roughly $1M+ of year-one revenue per program, about 10x the parent's $75-150k sensor setup, with software-like margins after the model is built. Second revenue line: sell the control-index and price-effect research to counties, lenders and appraisers. Assumptions to test: 10-25% of homes sell within 10 years and only some at a shortfall; expected payout 10-30% of escrow.
non_obvious_insight: A guarantee is cheaper for the developer than a check and more persuasive to the neighbor, at the same time: the expected payout is only the shortfall on homes that actually sell at a loss, and unspent money returns, while residents receive the thing they said they wanted (protection of value, per Propmodo) instead of hush money. It also sidesteps the attribution trap that hurts the parent, because the trigger is a formula on public deed data, not a causal claim about a well or a hum. And it aligns incentives: every year the facility runs quietly is a year the developer's escrow is not drawn, so neighbors and developer want the same outcome. Making the developer the obligor also removes the insurance-law problem the parent's escrow payout faced.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: build the price-effect model on deed and MLS data around 3 existing clusters (for example Loudoun and Prince William VA and one Georgia or Texas site) using difference-in-differences against matched control neighborhoods, and publish 'what data centers actually do to nearby home prices' (this is both lead generation and the expected-payout estimate). Days 10-20: write a 2-page term sheet and a development-agreement rider; call the government-relations and general-counsel offices of 8-10 independent developers that have publicly offered checks, buyouts or community funds. Days 15-30: pitch two county attorneys with pending hearings; line up a corporate escrow agent and one title company. Target: a letter of intent for a 300-household pilot with a $1M escrow. Gate at 90 days: one signed pilot or one county condition, plus a counsel view that the developer-obligor structure is not insurance in that state.
lineage: mutation of I1172 ('Neutral Baselines and Neighbor Guarantees for Data Centers'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: KETOS (SHIELD / KELP data-center water monitoring), Aethair (Aethair PRO, Environet, Thiamis), Envirosuite (ASX:EVS), Kunak. White space: Nobody found sells the bundle, so the status is 'gap' and not 'open'. The sensor and baseline layer is not open: KETOS (about $45M raised) pitches an independent baseline for data centers, Aethair pitches pre-construction baselines, Envirosuite has community dashboards, and consultancies bundle baselines into permitting. The unserved wedge is what sits on top of the sensors. (1) A neutral administrator holding escrowed, tamper-evident data whose governance the county and community accept, unlike developer-hired consultants and unlike opposition-side groups such as CEDS. (2) The Neighbor Guarantee: an automatic, no-litigation payout to households from a developer-funded escrow when a pre-agreed trigger is hit. No vendor, insurer, county ordinance or developer program found does this. The nearest things are Franklin County, Indiana's draft rule (escrow for 24-hour emergency potable water to impacted neighbors, plus developer-funded monitoring wells), one-off buyouts and lump-sum checks. (3) A 10-year, multi-parameter (wells, noise, PM2.5, voltage) record packaged as a permit-condition template that regulators can adopt. Weak points: the sensor baseline will commoditize; attribution is hard, because well drawdown from drought or other pumping is indistinguishable from data-center drawdown unless the design uses upgradient control wells and pumping records; automatic payouts may look like insurance under state law; and developer counsel may resist a pre-committed payout as an admission of liability. Note: the web-search budget ran out before I could check Crunchbase/YC directly for a startup doing exactly the escrow-plus-parametric bundle, so 'nobody found' means no evidence in about 25 searches, not proof of absence. | How this version avoids them: KETOS, Aethair, Envirosuite, Kunak, Clarity, Larson Davis and Eno are all sensor or environmental-data vendors and none touches property value, so there is no overlap in product, buyer budget line or moat. Consultancies (TRC, Salas O'Brien) sell permitting studies, not a financial guarantee administered after approval. Prevolt and Jambo sell risk screens and engagement software, not a payout mechanism. CEDS is an opposition-side advisory group. The developer-run substitutes (NorthPoint checks, Mason County buyouts, Microsoft's Community-First pledge) are the budget we redirect, and they lack a neutral administrator and a pre-agreed formula. A web check found no productized, third-party-administered data-center property-value guarantee (wind-project guarantees are bespoke and appraiser-run); verify in week 1. Title and escrow firms could copy the mechanics but lack model neutrality and county-approved governance.

title: AP-Inbox Implant Reconciler for Spine ASCs
one_liner: Forward your implant vendor invoices to one email address. We match each to the surgery, the payer's carve-out clause and the 835, and reopen the claim the day the invoice lands, so implant cost stops going unpaid.
customer: Independent, surgeon-owned spine and pain-management (spinal cord stimulator) ASCs doing about 100-600 implant cases a year. They have a one-to-three-person in-house billing office, or an outsourced biller paid a percentage of collections, and no supply-chain analyst. The buyer is the administrator plus the surgeon-owner who signs off on distributions. Launch in one state through its ASC association so outreach is dense.
problem: The leak is not ignorance of carve-outs (Becker's has covered them since 2014). It is a hand-off race. The claim leaves billing days after surgery. The consignment vendor invoice lands in accounts payable weeks later, if it is ever tied to the case. Sticker-sheet lot numbers, invoice lines and payer attachment rules share no common ID. So the claim goes out at charges, posts as 'paid', and no system emits the event 'invoice arrived for a case already billed'. Corrected-claim and appeal windows then expire silently. Testable hypothesis for the first audits: a meaningful share of implant cases have a claim date earlier than the invoice date. Each miss is worth roughly $5k-30k, and Medicare ASC cases are excluded because they are not carved out.
solution: (1) Zero-integration intake. Vendor invoices are auto-forwarded from the AP inbox, QuickBooks or Bill.com. An LLM extracts line items (manufacturer, catalog, lot, UDI-DI, unit price). The case schedule or implant log comes as a CSV or photos of sticker sheets, and the ERAs are pulled from the clearinghouse. No EHR or practice-management integration. (2) Rule engine with a payer-clause library. Contract PDFs are LLM-extracted and human-verified once, then reused across every ASC with the same payer. For workers' comp and no-fault, the engine uses public state fee schedules, several of which pay implants at invoice cost plus a capped markup (verify per state). This removes the 'read every contract' scaling limit. (3) The trigger. When an invoice matches a case already billed at $0 or bundled, it auto-builds the payer-specific attachment packet and corrected claim or appeal, ranked by days left to timely filing. Coders file for the first year, then automation. (4) A weekly one-page 'implant cash gap' for the administrator: unmatched invoices, invoice lag by vendor, payers paying $0.
why_now: ASC volume is shifting toward device-heavy musculoskeletal cases. CMS's CY2026 ASC final rule (CMS-1834-FC) is reported to add more of them; verify the exact list. Becker's ran 'ASCs' implant cost problem' in March 2026 and 'payer terms ASCs can't miss' in July 2026. Payer AI payment-integrity tools now auto-zero claims that lack attachments. LLM invoice extraction, which used to need OCR templates per vendor, is now cents per invoice.
revenue_model: Lookback: 25% of cash actually collected on recovered carve-outs, over a 12-18 month lookback bounded by timely filing, with no fee if nothing is recovered. Then convert to $1.5-2.5k/month per ASC (or about $12 per implant case) for the invoice trigger and weekly digest. Hypothesis to prove in the audits: a 300-implant-case ASC with a 10% leak at about $8k a case is $240k a year, so about $60k of first-year contingency and $18-30k a year of recurring revenue. Fifty ASCs would be roughly $1M+ of ARR plus about $3M of one-time contingency.
non_obvious_insight: The missing thing is an event, not data. Every RCM tool is triggered from the billing side, and nothing in the stack fires when an invoice arrives in AP after the claim is gone. Accounts payable is also the cheapest integration surface in healthcare, since forwarding email needs no IT project, so time-to-first-dollar is days. The wedge also counter-positions against billers. A percentage-of-collections biller cannot sell 'your billing is incomplete' without indicting itself, and the AP-side product never asks to replace them.
first_30_days: Week 1: DM or call 40 spine/SCS ASC administrators and surgeon-owners in one state via its ASC association and LinkedIn, offering a free 12-month lookback at 25% of cash collected only. Sign 3 design partners with a BAA. Week 2: pull 12 months of 835s, case and implant logs, and the AP invoice folder. Extract invoices with an LLM and spot-check to at least 95% line accuracy. Hand-read each site's top 3 commercial carve-out clauses. Week 3: match and measure three things. These are the share of implant cases where the claim predates the invoice, the implant lines paid $0 or bundled where the clause says carve-out, and the dollars still inside timely filing. Week 4: file the first 15-25 corrected claims and appeals, write a one-page anonymized leak report, and start outbound to 40 more ASCs. Gate: continue only if at least 2 of 3 sites show identifiable, collectible leakage of at least 3% of implant spend. Otherwise narrow to newly opened or converted ASCs, or kill.

competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Aspirion (ContractIQ, payment variance recovery), FinThrive (Contract Manager, A/R Optimizer, Revenue Integrity), Sift Healthcare (RevProtect), Waystar (Claim Attachments, Denial Recovery, Recoupment Manager). White space: Caveat on confidence: the WebSearch budget was exhausted (200/200) before any of my searches ran, so the competitor check is thinner than requested. It rests on direct fetches of about 15 vendor and trade-publication pages plus Becker's ASC on-site search result pages. The Becker's article bodies returned 403. Crunchbase, Reddit and Product Hunt were not reachable. I found no dedicated competitor doing what this idea describes, and I could not check the many small RCM and consulting shops that a live web search would surface. I also could not confirm Cloudmed/R1 or Experian Contract Manager features (the R1 URL 404'd). Both are plausible incumbents with contract modeling.

What looks unserved, and is specific: (1) a contingency service focused only on the implant/device carve-out. It would join the OR implant log (manufacturer, catalog and lot numbers) to the AP vendor invoice, then to the payer contract carve-out clause, then to the 835 line. None of the general underpayment vendors above advertise this. (2) The buyer is the physician-owned spine/ortho ASC. Enterprise tools like Sift, FinThrive and Aspirion are aimed at health systems. (3) The claim-side fix is assembling the invoice attachment per payer rules and filing a corrected claim inside timely-filing limits. General contract-modeling tools mostly stop at flagging a variance.

Risks to the premise:
- 'Nobody connects them' is overstated. Becker's ran 'ASC Implant Carve-Outs: Opportunities, Challenges & 4 Best Practices' in 2014, so ASC operators know carve-outs exist (https://www.beckersasc.com/asc-coding-billing-and-collections/asc-implant-carve-outs-opportunities-challenges-4-best-practices/). ASC-specialist billers such as SIS/Surgical Notes, National Medical Billing Services and Nimble probably submit implant invoices as routine, so the addressable leakage may sit mostly in ASCs with weak or outsourced generalist billing.
- Any player with a contingency model and payer-contract modeling could add this quickly. Aspirion's ContractIQ is the most obvious.
- Medicare does not carve out implants in the ASC setting, so this is a commercial-contract play only. Each payer contract must be read individually, which limits how far it scales.
- I could not verify the CY2026 IPO-list phase-out and ASC list additions cited in the idea's why-now. CMS's page confirms only that a CY2026 ASC final rule (CMS-1834-FC) exists. | How this version avoids them: Aspirion (ContractIQ), FinThrive Contract Manager, Sift RevProtect, Waystar and MDaudit all start from claims and contract models sold to hospital revenue-cycle teams. None ingest vendor AP invoices or fire on invoice arrival, and they are retrospective variance tools, not per-case attachment and corrected-claim builders. This product is sold to the ASC owner and administrator as a supply-chain-to-cash control, which those enterprise sellers do not reach. SIS/Surgical Notes and HST Pathways sit in the practice-management and billing workflow that this product deliberately stays outside, so it works with any biller or PM system. Defensibility comes from the cross-ASC payer-clause library and invoice-lag dataset, which is a cornered resource, and from the switching cost of becoming the ASC's implant ledger. If Aspirion bolts on contract-level carve-outs, it still needs the AP-side intake and the ASC-owner sale.

title: Sold-Out-of-Trust Radar for Floorplan Lenders
one_liner: Catch dealers that sell floored cars and pocket the payoff by watching the one signal an F&I insider knows can't be hidden: the VIN disappears from public listings but the floorplan payoff never arrives.
customer: Floorplan lenders and their auditors: independent floorplan companies, captive finance arms, regional banks and credit unions with dealer lines, and warehouse lenders that fund subprime and buy-here-pay-here dealers. Pay $15 to $30 per monitored dealer per month plus enterprise data fees.
problem: A dealer sells out of trust when it sells a floored car and does not pay the lender's payoff on time. It is how small cash squeezes become fraud. Ford and Stellantis are in court against Sky Auto Mall over exactly this, and floorplan use is heavier with inventory at roughly 88 days' supply and rates at SOFR plus 200 to 400 bps. Lenders police it with periodic on-site audits (monthly, quarterly or random), so a dealer can sell for weeks before anyone looks. The dealer's own delay makes it worse, since contracts in transit stretch to a week or more before the lender funds, so honest and dishonest dealers look identical in the books.
solution: Daily VIN-level monitoring of each lender's floored inventory against public and licensed listing feeds from the dealer's site and the major marketplaces. When a floored VIN disappears from listings, the tool starts a clock. It cross-checks against lender-provided payoff events and, where available, title and registration transactions and electronic lien releases. If no payoff shows within the expected window (about 7 to 10 days for a clean deal, longer for slow lenders), it flags the dealer and VIN and ranks risk by dealer history and how many VINs are in the queue. Flags trigger a spot audit or a curtailment call. A dealer-facing version shows honest dealers exactly which VINs look 'unpaid' so they can fix processing before the lender calls, and it doubles as an early-warning feed for warehouse lenders.
why_now: Sept 2025's Tricolor and PrimaLend collapses put double-pledged collateral and verification failures in front of every subprime lender and their investors. In March 2026 Ford and Stellantis were still litigating floorplan fraud against Sky Auto Mall. Rising inventory and higher rates increase floorplan reliance. Public listing feeds and cheap LLM data extraction make VIN-level monitoring practical for a team of three.
revenue_model: Per-dealer monthly monitoring fee, a per-alert fee on confirmed cases, and enterprise data licensing to captives and ABS or warehouse investors. Upsell: a contracts-in-transit tracker that gives dealers a lender-verified funding timeline and later powers same-day advances against verified contracts.
non_obvious_insight: The only place SOT cannot hide is the retail listing. A dealer will lie about payoffs, backdate titles and pay one lender with another's money, but it still has to take a car off its website when it sells it, because customers and marketplaces punish stale listings. Auditors check what is on the lot; nobody checks what left the internet. An F&I person knows this from watching sold cars vanish from the site the same day the deal is signed, and from knowing how long a funded payoff should really take.
first_30_days: Build a scraper for a pilot set of 50 dealer inventory pages and a listing-history log. Backtest on cases visible in public court filings (the Sky Auto Mall filings and a handful of others) to show the signal would have fired weeks earlier. Approach three small independent floorplan lenders and two credit unions with dealer floorplan lines, offer a free 60-day pilot on their books, and charge $20 per dealer per month after proving at least one real catch.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: In-house 'website VIN vs floorplan VIN' comparison (SAS Global Forum paper, 'PROC HTTP: Using the Web to Combat Fraud in Auto Finance During a Global Pandemic'), Vero Technologies (VeroOS), SBS Digital Audit (SBS Software), LotCount. White space: Among the products I could find, none sells the specific signal in this idea: an external-behavior signal (a floored VIN vanishing from the dealer site or marketplaces) checked against the lender's own payoff ledger on a running clock, with a ranked daily queue. Existing offerings cover other things. Physical or photo audits (CSI, LotCount, SBS Digital Audit, Netresult) are periodic and dealer-cooperative. Platforms (Vero, Solifi, Alfa, SBS servicing) analyze the lender's own payment and title data. Bank-data tools (Plaid-style) watch dealer cash. DRN covers location. The unserved wedge is mid-size and small lenders that lack data-science teams: independent floorplan companies, credit unions and community banks with dealer lines, and third-party audit firms that need risk-based audit targeting. It is strongest for used-car and buy-here-pay-here dealers, where captives' retail-delivery reports do not exist. Caveats that shrink the white space: (1) captives see retail deliveries within days and can build the signal in-house, and the SAS paper suggests at least one lender did; (2) Vero, SBS and Cox/NextGear could bolt on the signal; (3) a listing that disappears is a noisy signal (wholesaled, transferred, in recon, or the dealer never lists), so precision must be proven; (4) marketplace scraping has terms-of-service risk, so a licensed feed such as MarketCheck is likely needed.

title: AI Exclusion Diff for Pro-Liability Renewals
one_liner: Forward a renewal quote or binder PDF and get, within 24 hours, a diff against the expiring policy, a breadth score for any new AI exclusion, and a client-ready gap letter. It is built for the professional-liability desk of independent agencies, and it also ranks competing quotes by exclusion breadth.
customer: The professional-services desk at independent agencies of 8-60 staff. That means the producer or account manager who handles 60-120 E&O, tech E&O, D&O, cyber and pro-services CGL renewals a year for architects and engineers, accountants, law firms, marketing and design agencies, and IT and software services firms. Much of their paper is surplus lines placed through wholesalers, which SERFF-based tools cannot see.
problem: AI exclusions on professional-liability paper are the broadest and most bespoke (Berkley's 'absolute' PC 51380, 'any AI' versus gen-AI only, vendor-supplied AI, BI/PD versus advertising injury, manuscript wording). They arrive buried in a stack of quote and binder PDFs, and the premium barely moves. The producer has about 10 minutes per renewal and no way to tell whether the exclusion is new, how wide it is, or whether it hits what the client actually does. Quandri and Zywave compare premium and limits. Patra checks 900+ points but is not AI-specific and does not diff against the expiring form. Filing trackers show what a carrier filed in a state, not what is attached to this client's policy.
solution: Intake is an email-in address with no AMS integration. The producer forwards the quote, binder or policy PDF plus the expiring policy. The output is a one-page report with five parts. (1) Diff: is an AI exclusion new, widened or unchanged versus expiring. (2) Breadth score of 0-5 across six dimensions: gen-AI only versus any AI, BI/PD versus advertising or personal injury, vendor-supplied AI, professional-services carve-outs, defence-cost treatment, and prior-acts effect. (3) A short 8-question client AI-use intake, which shows which of the client's real AI uses are now stranded. (4) A client-ready gap letter with a signed-acknowledgment page. (5) Quote-stage ranking: when the producer holds 2-4 competing quotes, it ranks them by exclusion breadth and drafts the exact carve-back request to send back, for example 'replace any-AI with gen-AI-only and carve out vendor-supplied AI'. Public filings (Trades Coverage, Certian, Gridex) are used only as a free auto-labeller for known forms. Delivery in the first months is LLM extraction plus a retired E&O underwriter reviewing every report. The output is a PDF plus JSON that files into Epic or Zywave as an attachment, so the product is a partner add-on and not a rival dashboard.
why_now: Renewals dated 1 Jan 2027 are the first big cycle after the ISO CG 40 47/40 48 forms and Berkley's absolute exclusion, and those quotes reach producers in Nov-Dec 2026, which is now. Trade press and associations (IA Magazine on 9 Sep 2026, Big I, Agents United) are telling agencies to review renewals for AI exclusions, but they give no tooling. Zywave's Advisor Agent, in early access since June 2026, is teaching agencies to expect renewal triage, and it does not read endorsements. Long-context PDF extraction on scanned binders is now cheap and reliable enough to do the classification at a cost of about $1 per document.
revenue_model: Pay per renewal at $150 for a standard quote diff and $450 for a multi-policy or manuscript diff. A $600/month plan includes 20 diffs. A $500 concierge audit on an agency's five largest accounts is the entry offer. Unit economics: about $1 of inference plus 15 minutes of reviewer time at about $60/hour gives roughly 85% gross margin on a $150 diff. This is my estimate: 1,000-2,000 US agencies run a real professional-liability desk, at 80 renewals a year that is $12-24k per agency, so 100 agencies is about $1.2-2.4M ARR. Referral revenue from affirmative markets is optional upside, and nothing depends on it, which answers the judges' doubt about the 10-15% commission.
non_obvious_insight: The thing a producer pays for is the ask, not the detection. Manuscript AI exclusions are negotiable, and a diff that says 'this wording is broader than the same carrier's competitor quote, ask for this replacement' turns a defensive letter into a shopping and negotiation tool that wins the account. The E&O-fear trigger also does not depend on the duty-to-advise law, which is weak in most states. Agencies that sell 'annual coverage reviews' assume a duty, and the signed acknowledgment turns that exposure into a documented file. The moat is not the public filings database. It is a labelled corpus of issued forms as attached to real quotes, including surplus lines, with outcome labels showing which carve-backs carriers actually granted. That corpus grows with every diff, and nobody can scrape it.

Days 8-20: collect each agency's last 3 renewals for its 5 biggest pro-liability accounts (about 150 documents) and run the manual-plus-LLM diff. Measure the hit rate, meaning the share of renewals containing an AI exclusion the producer had not flagged. Proceed if it is 30% or more, and treat under 15% as the kill signal. Days 15-30: sell the $500 concierge audit and convert each agency to per-diff pricing for its live Nov-Dec 1/1 renewals. Publish the breadth scale v0.1 with 20 anonymised specimen forms as free content, and open a developer-partner conversation with Zywave and the Epic marketplace.

Rosella and FurtherAI do generic policy comparison with no AI breadth score, no gap letter and no negotiation ask. SERFF vendors (InsuranceFiling, Filing360, FilingRamp) sell to compliance teams, and their data misses surplus lines.

title: Loss-Draft Clearance Standard for Mortgage Servicers
one_liner: Mortgage servicers and portfolio lenders pay a per-loan fee for verified smoke clearance. That verification gates the final release of insurance loss-draft funds and the end of forbearance on smoke-damaged standing homes. Lenders, not carriers, become the enforcer of a defensible standard.
customer: Loss-draft and disaster-recovery departments at mortgage servicers and subservicers with concentrated Altadena, Pasadena and Palisades books, plus community banks, credit unions and CDFIs around Pasadena and the Westside. Secondary buyers: escrow and title officers on standing-home sales. Homeowners and their PAs are the delivery channel, not the payer.
problem: Servicers hold insurance proceeds on mortgaged, smoke-damaged homes and typically release them in staged draws with a final holdback against completion inspections. For destroyed homes the milestones are objective (foundation, framing). For smoke there is no completion gate: the contractor says 'cleaned', the carrier's vendor says 'clean', and the owner says the house still makes the family sick. EFRU's roughly 50 remediated homes showed 63% with elevated lead and one third with asbestos, so a lender that releases the last draw on an unverified cleaning is funding continued collateral impairment. A servicer that withholds gets complaints and unhappy borrowers paying a mortgage plus rent. I have not verified how servicers handle this today, so this is the riskiest assumption to test first.
solution: A one-page, servicer-adoptable 'Smoke Clearance Acceptance Standard' covering sampling grid, threshold basis, chain of custody and lab accreditation, tied to AB 1795, AIHA and IICRC/RIA/CIRI references and versioned for DTSC's 2028-29 standards. Alongside it, a portal where the borrower's hygienist or remediator uploads results. We verify them (automated checks plus partner CIH-of-record review) and issue a machine-readable Clearance Verification (pass, fail, or specific deficiency list) that the servicer's loss-draft workflow accepts to release the final draw or convert a forbearance. A book-level ledger shows every loan in the burn perimeter, joined to parcels, with status: not tested, tested, remediating, cleared. Testing stays paid by the insurer under AB 1795 or by the borrower from claim proceeds. The servicer pays only for verification and monitoring.
why_now: AB 1795 (effective 1/1/2027) forces insurers to pay for testing and bars ALE termination before clearance, so a verified clearance event now exists in statute and can be a lender milestone. 13,000+ standing homes with smoke damage in the LA fires, many mortgaged, are hitting the remediation and final-draw stage through 2027. Meanwhile the state standard will not exist until 2028-29, and servicers adopt vendor standards faster than agencies write them.
revenue_model: Servicers pay $250-$450 per loan verified, usually recoverable as an inspection or protective-advance line they already charge, plus $2-$5 per loan per month for ledger monitoring on flagged loans. Community banks and credit unions pay a flat $15k pilot. Hygienists and remediators can pay $50 to have their evidence pack pre-checked against the standard, since a fail costs them time. Honest sizing: LA alone is roughly 13,000 homes x about 55% mortgaged x $350 x 1.5 verifications, or about $3.7M. The business is the repeatable template for post-disaster loss-draft verification (hurricane mold, flood, wildfire) across the US, not California smoke alone.
non_obvious_insight: The party with real power over whether a smoke repair is 'done' is not the carrier or the state. It is whoever holds the last check. Servicers already control disbursement, already buy standardized inspection work in bulk, and do not need to win the sampling-design argument. They need a pass/fail they can rely on. Lender incentives also align with policyholders (impaired collateral) and with carriers (fewer reopened claims and bad-faith suits), which neutralizes the parent's buyer conflict. If five servicers and credit unions accept the same evidence package, contractors and hygienists will produce to it, so the de facto standard is set by lenders.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: ask 5 public adjusters which servicers are sitting on their clients' checks, then hold 25 calls with loss-draft and disaster managers at about 10 servicers and 10 Pasadena-area banks and credit unions. The one question is what evidence would let you release the final draw on a smoke claim. Days 10-20: draft the one-page acceptance standard and get two CIHs and one toxicologist to endorse it publicly. Days 20-30: agree a paid pilot of 15-30 loans at about $300 with one credit union or servicer, and pre-check evidence packs for 10 borrowers referred by PAs. If no servicer says smoke draws are actually stuck, kill or pivot to escrow and title on resale.

competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Hygiene Technologies International (HygieneTech), Rimkus, Safeguard EnviroGroup (Brad Kovar), EHS Analytical Solutions. White space: Mostly assessment supply and free guidance are crowded, so the raw 'do smoke testing' and 'publish a protocol' layers are not white space. Dozens of CIH-led firms sell $2k-$4k+ assessments and clearance certificates. AIHA, IICRC/RIA/CIRI, Purdue and EFRU already publish free or cheap protocols. Safeguard EnviroGroup is already pitching a 'defensible framework' to carriers. State agencies (AB 1795 drafts) planned to certify IHs, contractors and labs, which undercuts the training-fee line.

Still unserved: (1) Carrier and TPA operations under AB 1795. Nobody offers a claim-level compliance layer with the 30-day inspection clock, an audit-ready sampling plan mapped to zones, chain-of-custody records and an evidence file, sold as software. Carriers are 'technically opposed' but must comply from 1/1/2027, and CAT surge capacity is the pain. (2) Sampling-design defensibility. The fight is over how many samples, where, and against what background, and no independent tool scores a sampling plan or existing IH report for adequacy, though this is what class actions and the Purdue review turn on. (3) A neutral, versioned crosswalk from AIHA/IICRC/40 CFR 745.227 lead-dust levels and 8 CCR 1529 asbestos to a per-home plan, which updates when DTSC issues standards in 2028-29. (4) Pooled, structured sampling data across claims, which is what regulators reuse. EFRU holds only a few dozen homes.

Two facts weaken the 'vacuum' framing. Interim lead and asbestos thresholds already exist in AB 1642 (40 CFR 745.227(e)(8)(viii) and 8 CCR 1529). The vacuum is mainly sampling design and non-lead contaminants such as cyanide, other metals and dioxins.

Structural risks: the buyer conflict, because carriers may not adopt a protocol seen as policyholder-friendly and policyholder-side buyers want a testifying CIH rather than software. Remote IH sign-off and technician-collected samples may run into CIH and certification expectations. Any advantage is capped at the moment DTSC publishes standards.

Research limits: my web-search budget ran out before I could run Crunchbase, YC and TechCrunch-specific queries. The general startup searches (wildfire smoke assessment startup, chain-of-custody kits, technician network) found only wildfire-detection companies (Pano AI, FireScan, FireSafe AI), none in post-fire smoke-damage assessment. Treat 'no funded startup' as probable, not proven. | How this version avoids them: HygieneTech, Rimkus, Safeguard, EHS, Home BioTesting and Vert-type firms sell assessments to insurers and homeowners and none sells into loan servicing. They become the channel: the ones that produce evidence to our standard win a document lenders accept. Sedgwick and other carrier TPAs are structurally carrier-side, and a lender will not accept a carrier-side attestation as proof of collateral condition. The IICRC and AIHA guides and the Purdue and EFRU resources are cited inside the acceptance criteria, so they are inputs, not rivals. The state's 2028-29 standards make our criteria more specific, not obsolete, because servicers still need a verification workflow. The adjacent risk is property-preservation and loss-draft inspection vendors, who lack IH capability. We would license the standard to them white-label rather than compete.

title: Independent Answer Key for Synthetic Respondents
one_liner: Invert the referee: a neutral scoring authority that holds fresh, verified-human ground truth, and scores synthetic-respondent and digital-twin vendors against it in quarterly pre-registered, sealed-prediction benchmarks.
customer: Two-sided. Vendors: synthetic-respondent, persona and digital-twin startups and the survey platforms adding synthetic boosts. Buyers: CPG, pharma and financial-services insights and innovation teams and research agencies being pitched 'AI respondents' and unsure whom to believe. Later: AI labs that need uncontaminated human-opinion evals.
problem: Synthetic-respondent vendors claim high accuracy on self-chosen benchmarks. Backtests against old polls leak, because published polls and concept-test norms are in the models' training data, and vendors can cherry-pick questions. Buyers have no neutral way to tell which claim is real before betting a launch decision on it. The parent evidence that agents pass 99.8% of attention checks shows LLM personas mimic humans on surface features, which cuts both ways: it enables fraud and it makes synthetic research plausible. Nobody holds fresh verified-human answers on questions asked after model cutoffs, with the vendor's predictions locked in beforehand.
solution: A predict-then-reveal benchmark. Each quarter, the firm and a buyer advisory board write about 80 novel questions and concepts, including anonymised buyer concept tests under NDA. Vendors submit hash-committed sealed predictions of the answer distributions for named demographic targets. The firm fields the items to 1,000-3,000 verified humans, address-recruited and device-attested, licensed from partners (NORC, Verasight, Prolific or a university survey centre) so no one panel controls the answer key. It scores distribution error, rank-order of concept winners, subgroup fidelity and calibration of stated uncertainty, and publishes a leaderboard. Vendors pay for private diagnostics and for a licence to cite their scored accuracy, never for placement. Buyers pay for full reports and for a 'bake-off as a service', running a shortlist of 3 vendors on 10 of the buyer's own concepts against 400 verified humans. Endgame: the growing library of pre-registered human ground truth becomes shared infrastructure. It calibrates hybrid human-plus-synthetic samples, is licensed to AI labs as fresh opinion evals, and feeds the original bot-audit business off the same panel.
why_now: Synthetic-respondent and digital-twin companies raised large rounds in 2025-26 and are getting enterprise pilots (specific rounds not verified in this session, so check). Model releases every few months make static benchmarks stale and leaky, which turns a benchmark into a recurring re-fielding business. Pew's Aug 2026 study is a public design template for benchmarking against address-recruited samples. Buyers who lived through the panel-fraud scare now ask 'how do you know it is right?' by reflex.
revenue_model: Vendors pay $8-25k per quarterly private diagnostic and $30-100k/yr for an audited accuracy-claim licence. Buyers pay $10-25k/yr for full reports and $20-40k per bake-off. Founding-member pre-sales fund wave 1: 8 buyers at $15k covers a 1,000-human wave. Later, AI-lab dataset licences of $100-500k/yr. Control-panel cost is the main COGS at about $10-40 per verified complete, which suggests 60-70% gross margin once pre-sales cover each wave.
non_obvious_insight: The verified-human panel is worth more as the answer key for AI than as a shield against AI, and the business wins whichever way the synthetic-research bet goes. If synthetic respondents work, everyone needs a scorer and a calibration anchor. If they fail, buyers need proof and a return to human samples. Fraud and progress both raise demand for the reference. The product is not data but a commitment protocol (sealed predictions, then reveal), which solves the training-data leakage that no static dataset can. Refusing to be scored becomes a signal of weakness, which is the flywheel that turns a benchmark into a standard, the way MLPerf-style or leaderboard-style evaluators gained authority.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: write the protocol and scoring spec (sealing method, metrics, no pay-for-placement rule) and publish it openly. Recruit 5 founding buyer-side advisors (CPG or pharma insights heads) at $5k pilot memberships. Days 5-20: invite 6-8 synthetic-respondent vendors to a free founding wave slot in exchange for submitting sealed predictions. Days 15-30: finalize 40 novel questions, hash-commit vendor predictions, and field wave 0 to 600-1,000 verified humans from a partner for roughly $10-20k. Publish the first leaderboard by day 45. Kill test: fewer than 4 vendors willing to submit, or fewer than 3 buyers who say they would pay for the results.
lineage: mutation of I0716 ('Independent Referee for Survey Panel Data'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Data Quality Co-op (DQC), Verasight, Verisoul, CloudResearch (Sentry, Engage, Bot Olympics). White space: Detection is crowded and getting cheap: Verisoul, Roundtable, dtect, CloudResearch, Kantar Qubed, Research Defender, PureScore, ReDem and CleanID all sell it, some at cents per respondent. Cross-supplier scorecards already exist too, since Data Quality Co-op is a neutral clearinghouse. Building a detection ensemble or a generic vendor scorecard would be a fifth-to-tenth entrant against funded players.

What I did not find anyone selling:
1. A per-study ground-truth calibration. This means running a slice of the same questionnaire on a verified, address-recruited human control group and then reporting contamination-adjusted estimates with error bounds. Every vendor I found detects and removes. None quantifies how much bias survives the cleaning, and none re-estimates the result against a known-real reference. Pew's finding that voter-file matching removed valid respondents and made the error worse suggests 'remove the flagged' is itself a source of bias.
2. A neutral buyer-side referee that owns no sample. dtect is neutral but only sells entry-time detection. DQC is neutral but does not audit individual studies or supply a control sample. Verasight owns verified humans but sells sample.
3. Independent, third-party verification of the vendors' own accuracy claims. CloudResearch and Verisoul each claim 100% agent detection from internal or self-run tests. The Bot Olympics is MIT-judged but tests CloudResearch's own system.

The missing piece for a startup is the control panel. Building an address-recruited, device-attested panel of about 2,000 people is slow and expensive. The likelier route is to partner with or license an existing one (Verasight, NORC, Pew or Ipsos-style panels), not recruit from scratch.

This conclusion has limits. My WebSearch budget ran out at 200 calls, so I could not run the Crunchbase, YC or Product Hunt checks or search for a second wave of small startups. I also could not confirm funding for DQC, Roundtable, dtect or Verasight. | How this version avoids them: Every competitor in the parent's research defends human samples against bots (Verisoul, dtect, Roundtable, CloudResearch, Kantar Qubed, PureScore, ReDem) or sells verified sample (Verasight), or writes standards without testing (GDQ). None scores synthetic respondents. CloudResearch's Bot Olympics grades detectors on its own turf and is not neutral. Verasight's replication of Pew shows its own panel is cleaner, so it sells sample and could not be an arbiter between vendors that compete with its product. DQC is neutral but aggregates fraud signals. It does not run sealed-prediction tests against fresh human truth. Pew and NORC could field this, but a non-profit research org will not run a recurring commercial scoring service. Academic synthetic-survey benchmarks exist but are static and leak into training data. I could not verify whether a commercial neutral scorer already exists because the web-search budget ran out, so check before building.

title: Independent Audit Samples for Modeled Lead Inventories
one_liner: Become the independent auditor of predictive lead-line inventories: sell engineering consultants and state reviewers a statistically designed sample of 60-150 photo-verified lines that proves a model's error rate, paid per ground-truth point plus an annual attestation fee.
customer: Regional engineering and environmental consulting firms (50-500 staff) that win lead-line inventory work as prime contractor, license or run a predictive model, and must defend the classification to a state reviewer. Wedge: firms holding three or more utility inventory contracts in a state whose drinking-water program requires field validation of modeled non-lead classifications, or in a state that rejects pure modeling (Texas is reported not to accept predictive modeling for official inventories, verify before selling). The state reviewer is the second beneficiary, and the utility is the eventual budget owner.
problem: Predictive modelers and consultants classify tens of thousands of unknown lines statistically, but a regulator or council will ask 'what is your error rate?' The consultant's current answer is a field crew, a subcontractor or potholing, priced at hundreds of dollars per point, with no independence from the party selling the model. Vendors that sell both prediction and verification are grading their own homework. In the parent idea the buyer was a utility that needed tens of thousands of lines cleared, which made low homeowner response and thin supply fatal. An audit needs far fewer points.
solution: An audit-sample service. We draw a stratified random sample from the utility's modeled bins (predicted non-lead, predicted lead, low-confidence), so the sample design is ours and can't be steered by the modeler. Homeowners get a utility-letterhead notice with a $25-30 incentive. A panel of 20-40 licensed plumbers and inspectors in the state visit and capture the three-photo protocol plus scratch and magnet test. Each point goes through AI classification, human QA, and tamper-evident geo-verification. Deliverables: (1) an evidence pack in the state inventory format; (2) an error-rate report with confidence intervals, including a non-response follow-up on a subset to measure bias; (3) a signed attestation the consultant can attach to the inventory submission. Where the state requires water-system oversight, the utility designates panel members as its agents in writing or witnesses by video. The sampling math is what makes it small: if 60 randomly sampled 'non-lead' lines are all non-lead, the true lead rate in that bin is below 5% with 95% confidence, and 150 clean lines bounds it below 2%.
why_now: First-round inventories leaned heavily on models, and reviewers, litigants and journalists are now questioning the unknown and 'non-lead' bins. The next inventory update cycle (around late 2027 under the federal rule, verify) is when models get challenged. Consultants are under fixed-fee pressure and want to avoid running field crews. Vision models plus tamper-evident capture make a small distributed audit panel cheaper than centrally staffed crews. Predictive modeling has reached the point where the constraint is credibility, not accuracy.
revenue_model: Wholesale price of about $140 per ground-truth point, against a cost of roughly $85-95 (panel payout $70-85, homeowner incentive, QA). An audit of one bin (60-150 points) is $9-21k, and a mid-size utility with three bins is a $30-40k engagement that fits under many small-purchase limits. Sold through the consultant as a pass-through with markup, or directly to the utility when the state reviewer requests it. Recurring revenue comes from an annual drift attestation ($10-15k per utility) as inventories are updated. A later product is a labeled, consented evidence dataset licensed back to modelers to retrain.
non_obvious_insight: A buyer that needs a sample, not a census, changes everything the judges worried about. Sixty to a few hundred points per utility means a 10-25% response rate is fine, thin opportunistic supply is fine, and per-point price can be $140 instead of $40. Every clean point vouches for thousands of predicted lines, so a sample point is worth far more to the buyer than a census point. The valuable thing to sell is independence: the model vendor cannot audit its own model, and the consulting firm that sells hourly field crews has no reason to keep the audit small.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: interview 10 regional consulting firms and 3 state drinking-water programs. Ask what evidence the state wants to accept a modeled non-lead bin, and whether a third-party photo sample with utility authorization counts. Pick one state and one consultant with at least three active inventory contracts. Days 10-25: recruit 20 licensed inspectors and plumbers through local chapters and pay a launch rate. Draw a random sample of 60 from one predicted non-lead bin the consultant has already produced. Mail notices with the incentive and contact until 60 are visited. Days 25-30: deliver the evidence pack and a one-page error-rate memo at cost or free, and submit it to the state reviewer through the consultant. Ask for a paid audit of the next utility's three bins.

title: Port-Level IP Shield for Indie Brands
one_liner: A subscription that registers small brands' trademarks and copyrights with CBP, feeds officers product-identification guides, and turns port detentions into evidence and settlements against the importers.
customer: Indie consumer brands with $1-30M in revenue that get cloned: fashion, toys, beauty, pet, home goods and Shopify DTC brands. They pay a monthly subscription, plus a share of any enforcement settlements.
problem: Small brands fight knockoffs with Amazon Brand Registry and platform takedowns. Those work after the goods have landed and the listings are live. Most never use the cheapest lever, which is CBP itself. Recording a mark or copyright with CBP e-Recordation costs about $190 per class. CBP can then detain suspected counterfeit or lookalike shipments at the port, and the rights-holder can get photos, samples and importer details that support demand letters and lawsuits. In practice, small brands rarely record. When CBP does ask for authentication, the brand replies late, so the goods are released.
solution: 'Port Shield' handles recordation, builds a product-identification guide (photos, tells, label details, authorized-factory MID list) that officers can use, and monitors for CBP detention and seizure notices. It answers authentication requests within CBP's short response windows, and sets up lever-rule protection against gray-market goods where it applies. It also runs a port exposure scan: lookalike listings on marketplaces matched against public bill-of-lading data to find who is shipping them into LA/Long Beach. When CBP detains a shipment, it packages the importer identity and evidence for partner IP counsel to send demand letters, and takes a share of settlements.
why_now: Generative AI has made cloning product photos and standing up dupe storefronts nearly free, so knockoff volume against small brands is rising. The 2025 de minimis clampdown, and the statutory repeal scheduled for July 2027, push formerly parcel-shipped knockoffs into entries CBP can actually target and hold. Tariff-era entries also carry much richer line-level data, which improves targeting. Long Beach hit a record August of 919,992 TEUs, so port volume is not shrinking.
revenue_model: $750 setup, then $299-$799 a month by number of marks and product lines. Enforcement adds a 20-30% share of settlements, and IP counsel pays referral fees. A later tier sells port-level counterfeit intelligence to marketplaces and insurers.
non_obvious_insight: CBP can only hold what the rights-holder helps it verify. Officers see thousands of lookalikes and act on brands that have recorded marks, supplied identification guides and answered inquiries fast. Big brands have law firms doing this. Sub-$30M brands do not know the port is a free enforcement layer, and most of the relevant customs rules are written for lawyers, not founders.
first_30_days: Pick two crowded niches, such as LA-based apparel and accessories and Shopify beauty or pet. Run free port exposure scans on 30 brands by matching lookalikes to importers in public BOL data. Cold-email the brand owners with the scan attached. (6) Lever-rule (19 CFR 133.23, https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/19/133.23) covers gray-market goods that are physically and materially different; it does not address knockoffs and is a niche add-on.

title: Verified AI Coverage Levels for Vendor Contracts
one_liner: Invert the parent by checking the vendor's insurance from the counterparty's side. AI-enabled vendors upload their policies and get an independent, shareable 'AI Coverage Level' (L0-L3) with monitoring, so enterprise procurement teams can write 'L2 or higher' into contracts. Over time that makes it the insurance-sufficiency standard for AI vendors.
customer: Payer: AI-enabled software and services vendors of 10-300 staff (SaaS with AI features, dev and marketing agencies, MSPs, fintech and health-tech vendors) who sell to banks, health systems and other regulated enterprises with insurance clauses in their MSAs. Free users: enterprise general counsel, TPRM and procurement teams. Later payers: those enterprises' portfolio-monitoring subscriptions, and vendor-compliance and trust-center platforms embedding the check by API.
problem: Enterprise MSAs require vendors to carry, for example, $5M tech E&O and $5M cyber. Proof is a certificate of insurance, which shows limits, carrier and expiry but not exclusions. An absolute AI exclusion in the E&O policy makes the certificate hollow for exactly the failures the buyer worries about (a hallucinated output that costs money, model-vendor data leakage, generated-content IP claims, an autonomous action). The vendor rarely knows, because the broker did not flag the endorsement. The buyer relies on coverage nobody has read, and the indemnity is only as good as the vendor's balance sheet. The insured is the party least motivated to find out its coverage is hollow, so it never gets found. (I could not run web checks in this session to confirm that no COI tracker already reads endorsement wording, so treat that as an assumption to verify first.)
solution: First product, sellable within 6 months: the 'AI Coverage Attestation'. The vendor or its broker uploads the policies and endorsements, and the same diff and classification engine runs. An independent reviewer signs a one-page output. It shows the level and, for four AI failure modes (erroneous output, IP infringement from generated content, data leakage through a model provider, autonomous action), whether each is covered, excluded or silent, plus retro date and whether defence costs sit inside limits. The vendor gets a shareable live link for procurement teams and trust centers. Monitoring re-verifies at every renewal or cancellation and alerts the vendor and anyone who holds the link. The published levels run from L0 (absolute or any-AI exclusion), L1 (gen-AI exclusion with carve-backs), L2 (silent, with no AI exclusion) to L3 (affirmative AI cover). The buyer gets a free portal and an 'AI insurance rider' clause library, so a GC can write 'vendor must hold L2 or higher' into an MSA. Vendors at L0 or L1 are given a neutral list of affirmative markets, but nothing in the model depends on placement.
why_now: Enterprise AI procurement is now standard, and AI addenda in MSAs and security questionnaires are spreading. Vendors renewing on 1 Jan 2027 will be the first large cohort to lose AI coverage silently, just as customers' contracts assume it. Trades Coverage counted 2,369 AI exclusions in force by 31 July 2026, so the exposure exists at scale. Trust-center tools have made 'share evidence by link' the normal way to close security reviews, and AIUC-1 shows that buyers accept an AI assurance standard when it is credible. Long-context extraction over policy PDFs is what makes independent attestation affordable.
revenue_model: Vendor pays $900-2,400 per year per attestation including monitoring, or $250 for a rush one-off when a deal is waiting. Enterprise portfolio monitoring for 200+ vendors is $12-30k per year. Platform API checks are $20-60 each. Affirmative-market referral fees are a later, secondary line. These are estimates to test. The payer is the vendor, because a tick-box that blocks a six-figure deal is worth far more than the fee.
non_obvious_insight: This flips the buyer chain. The party that relies on the coverage, and holds contractual leverage, is the one who can force a hundred vendors to verify, so the value of the credential rises with each buyer that references it. That is a network effect broker software does not have. It also sidesteps the duty-to-advise weakness, because the obligation is contractual, not tort-based. And the level scheme lets an independent attestor become the standard, while carriers cannot credibly grade their own wording and the AI-liability carriers have a conflict.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: interview 20 vendor CFOs and founders and 10 GC or TPRM leads, and collect 5 real security questionnaires or MSAs that contain an AI-insurance question. Days 8-20: run 10 free attestations on real policies from vendors who agree, and publish Levels v0.1 with one redline rider clause. Days 15-30: pre-sell 5 attestations at $500 to vendors with a live deal blocked on the question, and pitch 2 trust-center or COI platforms for a pilot integration. Kill signal: if fewer than 3 of the 20 buyers can name a deal or contract review where the insurance question mattered, the counterparty pull is not there.

title: Town-Paid Private Road Census and Formation Bounty
one_liner: Sell New England towns (and their municipal insurance pools) a four-week census of every private road's legal status and emergency-access risk, then earn a per-road bounty for each neighbor group converted into a recorded association with a named point of contact.
customer: Town managers, road commissioners and fire chiefs of small and mid-sized Maine towns (2,000-15,000 residents), then NH and VT. Multi-town buyers: regional councils and planning commissions, and municipal risk pools that fund loss-control services for member towns (Maine Municipal Association's risk program, NH Primex, Vermont VLCT PACIF, all from prior knowledge and unverified here). Secondary payers: developers, via a road-association setup line on the town's subdivision application fee. Residents co-pay a small share.
problem: Every town has dozens to hundreds of private ways with unknown legal status. The town usually cannot spend public money on them (varies by state, to be confirmed per state), yet it is blamed when an ambulance or plow cannot pass a failed culvert, when a subdivision road approved on the condition that a road association be formed decays years later, or when residents petition the town to accept a broken road that would cost six figures to rebuild to town standard. After a storm, state aid wants an organized counterparty. NC's post-Helene private-road program (verified) required a single point of contact and proof of ownership, plus a 50% cost share. The town has no inventory to hand over. Neighbors are stuck in a collective-action deadlock, because nobody wants to be the one who calls the meeting.
solution: Step 1, a fixed-price Private Road Census, roughly $6,500 per town. We ingest parcel GIS, E911 road-name files, registry-of-deeds documents and any culvert or bridge inventory the town has. Language models read the recorded instruments to flag whether a maintenance agreement exists and what it says. For each private way we output parcels served, recorded instrument yes/no, whether an active association exists, contact if any, single-access and stream-crossing flags, and a fire-truck-passability risk score reviewed with the fire chief. The town gets a ranked list, map and memo. Step 2, activation. The town mails a letter on its own letterhead to the top 40 roads with a pre-filled petition for the statutory meeting. In Maine a few owners can petition a notary, and the town letter breaks the who-goes-first deadlock. We run the meetings, and an attorney-supervised covenant is recorded. The town pays a $600 bounty for each completed association (recorded instrument plus officers and point of contact), and residents co-pay about $500. Step 3, a registry subscription at about $2,400 per town per year. It keeps contacts, insurance certificates, reserve attestations and condition photos current, and yields a disaster-ready roads list for the state emergency agency after a storm. Step 4, the town adds a setup fee to subdivision applications so new roads get an association and reserve schedule at approval.
why_now: The cost stack collapsed. Reading recorded instruments for 120 roads used to mean about 120 title searches at hundreds of dollars each. With document extraction plus human QA it is roughly a tenth of that, which is what makes a fixed-price census possible. Storm events keep exposing the same gap, and NC's $175M program (verified) shows states will pay for repair but only through an organized counterparty. Parcel GIS and E911 layers are now open in most New England states. Municipal risk pools are always looking for loss-control programs to justify member subsidies (hypothesis to test). The disaster-aid windows (NC applications closed Feb 2026) show that the next program will again favor roads that are already organized.
revenue_model: Census $6,500 per town, or a regional-council package of 10-12 towns at about $55-65k. Formation bounty $600 per association from the town, plus a $500 resident co-pay, or about $1,100 per road. Registry $2,400 per town per year. Developer setup fee about $1,200 per new subdivision, collected through the town. A town with 120 private ways where 60% are informal has about 70 candidates. If 40% convert in year 1, that is 28 roads, about $31k in bounties and co-pays, plus census and registry, or about $40k per town in year 1. 25 towns would be about $1M. Conversion rate is the key hypothesis. Risk pools could subsidize the census for members, making the insurer a second payer.
non_obvious_insight: The town is not buying road repairs or software. It is buying a legal counterparty for roads it cannot touch, plus a defensible record that it knew about the risk and acted. That is liability hygiene, an easier budget line than subsidizing private roads. The official letter is the cheapest neighbor-activation channel that exists, because it dissolves the who-goes-first deadlock that makes formation so slow closing-by-closing. One buyer delivers dozens of roads, which inverts the parent's per-road CAC. The census data, once assembled across towns, becomes a state-level inventory that emergency agencies, lenders and title underwriters would pay for.
first_30_days: Pick one pilot town with open parcel GIS and online registry access, ideally a lakes-region Maine town of about 4,000 people. Build a free 30-road slice of the census in 10 days from public data. Walk it to the road commissioner, fire chief and town manager, and ask them for the 5 roads they fear most. Ask to mail an official letter to 10 pilot roads and run 2 statutory meetings within 30 days. In parallel, call 3 regional councils and the risk-management teams of the Maine, NH and Vermont municipal associations to test whether they would subsidize census work as loss control. Target one signed $4,500 first-town census (typically under small-purchase thresholds, to be confirmed) and one pilot association recorded. Riskiest assumptions: town willingness to pay a per-road bounty, and letter-to-meeting conversion above 25%.

title: 48-Hour Verify List for Independent Floorplan Lenders
one_liner: A daily, capacity-capped list of the specific floored VINs an independent lender's auditor should physically verify in the next 48 hours, built from listing disappearance plus the lender's own payoff ledger, with a disposition classifier and per-dealer baselines that fix the noisy-signal problem.
customer: Head of collateral or audit (CRO as signer) at independent used-car floorplan lenders with roughly $30M to $500M outstanding across 100 to 1,500 independent and buy-here-pay-here dealers, plus credit unions and community banks with dealer floorplan lines. It deliberately excludes franchised new-car dealers, where captives already get retail delivery reports and can build this in-house. Secondary channel is regional floorplan audit firms that dispatch for-cause audits.
problem: An independent lender has a handful of auditors and hundreds of dealers, so the Monday question is not 'is there fraud' but 'which 12 VINs at which 4 dealers do I visit this week'. The judges' flaws map onto this. (1) A raw 'VIN left the website' flag is noisy, since the car may be wholesaled, transferred to a sister lot, in recon or never listed. (2) A fixed 7 to 10 day payoff window misfires on slow-funding but honest dealers. (3) A standalone radar dashboard is one more screen for a team with no data scientists. (4) The $15 to $30 per dealer price is unvalidated. (5) It misses double-flooring, which was most of Sky Auto Mall.
solution: Data need is one file: the lender's daily list of active floored VINs (VIN, dealer, floor date, advance), exported as a flat file from any core system. A VIN dropping off that file means it was paid, so no payoff-event integration is needed. Listing history comes from a licensed feed (a MarketCheck-type source scanning 100k+ dealer sites daily), plus a crawl of only the lender's own dealers' public sites, which the lender's dealer agreement can require them to permit. (a) A disposition classifier sorts every vanished floored VIN into transfer to a sister store, appears at auction or wholesale, relisted, or 'retail-sale signature' (gone, no reappearance, often after a pending or price-change state). Only the last type with an open balance enters the queue. (b) Each dealer gets its own baseline lag distribution of delist-to-payoff days learned over 90 days, and the flag fires on deviation from that dealer's own pattern, not a fixed window. (c) The output is capped to the lender's audit capacity, for example 'you have 3 auditor-days: here are the 12 VINs at 4 dealers with the highest expected loss', with a timestamped listing-history evidence pack and a one-click verify request that can go to the lender's own auditors or an audit vendor. (d) An optional second signal is title or lien-release data where lawfully obtainable, but v1 does not depend on it.
why_now: Tricolor and PrimaLend (Sept 2025) and the Sky Auto Mall litigation (Ford Credit and Stellantis, March 2026) made every lender's risk committee ask what they know between audits. Inventory sits near 88 days' supply with floorplan at SOFR plus 200 to 400 bps, so dealers lean harder on lines. Licensed daily dealer-site listing history now exists off the shelf, and LLM extraction makes normalizing messy dealer pages cheap for a team of three. Vero's April 2026 content says bank dealer-services teams want to 'automate audit triage and SOT reporting', which confirms the buyer's framing.
revenue_model: Platform fee of about $1,500 to $3,000 per month per lender, sized to dealer count and booked against the audit budget, plus a catch fee of about $250 per VIN later confirmed unpaid-sold by the lender's own ledger and caught before its next scheduled audit. A backtest-based 'retro-scan' is priced at $5k and credited against year one. A lender with 300 dealers pays roughly $40k to $60k per year. A first-two-years target of 40 to 60 lenders and credit unions implies roughly $2M to $3.5M ARR. These are assumptions to validate, not findings.
non_obvious_insight: The lender's payoff ledger is free data hiding in plain sight: a VIN leaving the daily floored-VIN file is the payoff event, so the product needs one CSV, not a core-system integration. The real product is dispatch, not detection. Auditors only pay for a signal that changes whom they visit this week, and the noise is tamed by comparing each dealer to its own delist-to-payoff habits rather than to a global threshold, and by refusing to alert unless the disposition looks like a retail sale.
first_30_days: Weeks 1 to 2, backtest on public cases (Sky Auto Mall filings and a few others) using historical listing data to show fire dates versus discovery dates. In parallel, interview five lender audit or risk heads to confirm the ranked list would change their audit order. Weeks 2 to 4, sign three small independent floorplan lenders or credit unions to a free retro-scan. They send 12 months of daily floored-VIN files plus their known SOT events. Report recall, false alerts per 100 dealers per week and median days of lead time over their actual discovery. Offer a free 60-day live shadow run, converting to platform plus catch fee only after at least one real catch. Also ask two audit firms for a for-cause dispatch partnership.

title: Contingency Recovery of Unpaid Implant Carve-Outs
one_liner: Find and collect the implant and device carve-out payments that hospitals and surgery centers are owed but never bill, because the invoice lives in accounts payable and not in the billing office.
customer: Physician-owned spine and orthopedic ASCs, plus small and mid-size hospital ortho/spine/cardiac service lines, with commercial payer contracts that carve out implants. Paid 20-30% of recovered dollars.
problem: Many commercial contracts pay implants and high-cost devices separately, at invoice cost plus a markup, but only if the vendor invoice is submitted with the claim. The implant log is in the OR record, the invoice is in supply chain or AP, and the claim is built by billing. Nobody connects them. The claim goes out with L8699 or revenue code 027x lines at billed charges, and the payer pays $0 for the device or folds it into the case rate. The payment posts as 'paid', so nobody notices the loss. This is $5k-$50k per case for spine and joint work.
solution: Ingest the implant log (manufacturer, catalog and lot numbers), AP invoice PDFs (parsed with an LLM), contract carve-out terms extracted from the PDFs, and the 837/835 files. Compute expected carve-out payment versus actual, auto-assemble invoice attachments per payer rules, and file corrected claims and appeals inside timely-filing windows. Run it as a service for the first clients (manual, coder-led), then automate the matching.
why_now: CMS's CY2026 outpatient rule began phasing out the inpatient-only list and added many procedures, mostly musculoskeletal, to the ASC-covered list. More device-heavy spine and ortho cases are moving to ASCs whose small billing staffs have never dealt with carve-outs. Payers are also using AI-driven payment integrity that makes missing attachments an automatic zero.
revenue_model: 20-30% contingency on recovered carve-out payments. After the first recovery, convert to $1.5-4k/month prospective monitoring per facility.
non_obvious_insight: The loss is invisible in every standard revenue-cycle KPI. Denial rate looks fine and AR looks fine because the line paid 'as billed under the case rate'. The only way to see it is to lay the supply chain invoice next to the contract term next to the 835. Billers know it happens. Supply chain does not know payers pay for it. Finance never audits it. That gap between three departments is the earned secret.
first_30_days: Pick 10 physician-owned spine and ortho ASCs through ASCA chapters and surgeon-owner LinkedIn outreach. Offer a free 90-day lookback audit, since contingency means zero risk to them. Each needs to share 835s, implant logs, invoices and the top three commercial contracts. Do the first three audits by hand with a coder and a spreadsheet, and use the dollars found as the sales collateral. Then automate the invoice parsing.
