Risks to the premise:
- 'Nobody connects them' is overstated. Becker's ran 'ASC Implant Carve-Outs: Opportunities, Challenges & 4 Best Practices' in 2014, so ASC operators know carve-outs exist (https://www.beckersasc.com/asc-coding-billing-and-collections/asc-implant-carve-outs-opportunities-challenges-4-best-practices/). ASC-specialist billers such as SIS/Surgical Notes, National Medical Billing Services and Nimble probably submit implant invoices as routine, so the addressable leakage may sit mostly in ASCs with weak or outsourced generalist billing.
- Any player with a contingency model and payer-contract modeling could add this quickly. Aspirion's ContractIQ is the most obvious.
- Medicare does not carve out implants in the ASC setting, so this is a commercial-contract play only. Each payer contract must be read individually, which limits how far it scales.
- I could not verify the CY2026 IPO-list phase-out and ASC list additions cited in the idea's why-now. CMS's page confirms only that a CY2026 ASC final rule (CMS-1834-FC) exists.

title: One Binder Scan: Lender Monitoring Plus Warranty Recovery
one_liner: One AI read of a data hall's closeout binders yields both a lender's ready-for-service probability and an owner's serial-level warranty ledger, with contingency warranty recovery as the reason the owner grants access.
customer: Private credit funds, banks and insurers lending against GPUs and neocloud contracts (pay a fixed monitoring fee). Colo developers, powered-shell landlords and neocloud owners with energized but idle halls (pay a share of recovered warranty value).
problem: Lenders need interior truth about the last 90 days before ready-for-service but borrowers resist giving data-room access to a monitor. Owners of energized-but-empty halls don't know their OEM warranty clocks are silently running out. Both parties need the same documents (gear serials, startup sheets, Cx reports, integrated test results, punch lists) and neither has staff to read them.
solution: An LLM pipeline ingests POs, bills of lading, startup sheets, Cx sign-offs and maintenance logs into one serial-level ledger. Lender view: a Readiness Ladder score with probability of ready-for-service by date, covenant and draw triggers, and OEM startup-tech calendar risk. Owner view: warranty expiry dates, voiding conditions, and a hit list of claims and start-date deferrals to file within 90-120 days. Sold as a $25K two-week lender second opinion, made economical by a contingency warranty scan (25-30% of recoveries) offered free to the owner. Structure the two views as separate teams with an information wall, and route recoveries through the lender-controlled operating account so the independence of the monitor is not compromised.
why_now: About half of 2026 US capacity is slipping and neocloud credit is a live worry, so lenders are capping exposure. Many halls are powered, commissioned and idle. Equipment was bought at peak, tariff-inflated prices, so each lapsed warranty is worth more. Satellites have commoditized the exterior, leaving the interior (binders and commissioning data) as the scarce truth. LLMs now read messy closeout binders cheaply.
revenue_model: Lender side: $25K two-week second opinions, $40-120K full pre-close diligence, $8-20K per month per facility monitoring. Owner side: 25-30% of recovered value or avoided cost on claims and deferrals, $150-400 per asset per year tracking, $15-40K closeout audits, and PO-stage clause packs that defer warranty start to beneficial occupancy.
non_obvious_insight: The warranty ledger and the readiness score are built from the same binder, so the second product costs almost nothing to produce. The biggest barrier to interior monitoring is borrower cooperation, and a free contingency service that recovers money is the best incentive to provide it. Expiring warranties and unavailable OEM startup techs are also leading indicators of delay, so each product improves the other's signal. The lender's covenant becomes the distribution channel to owners at the moment they have binders and idle halls. Ethyco offers warranty-phase support but not idle-hall contingency or lender integration.
first_30_days: Recruit 6 retired or between-jobs Cx leads and PMs on 1099 contracts. Find 3 owner-operators through Cx and PM networks whose halls energized 8-11 months ago and are not fully loaded, and offer a free 10-day binder scan on contingency. Build the extraction on real binders (gensets, UPS and chillers first) and deliver an 'expiring in 90 days' hit list. Publish a free 'RFS credibility checklist' and pitch 5-10 private credit desks a $25K two-week second opinion on one live deal, using the scan as proof of depth.
lineage: hybrid of I0365 + I0229 (Ground-Truth Diligence for GPU-Backed Lenders + Warranty Clock Recovery Audits for Idle Halls). Why stronger: Double revenue from one document-processing pipeline, with two payers whose interests line up. Owners get paid to be monitored, lenders get better collateral and cleaner data, and access friction disappears. A serial-number equipment register across financed halls becomes a data moat that single-purpose competitors (satellite monitors or Cx firms) cannot replicate.
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: SynMax Vulcan (with Industrial Info Resources data partnership), Currence (formerly Sightline Climate), Epoch AI Frontier Data Centers Hub, SemiAnalysis (consulting, AI Datacenter Model, ClusterMAX). White space: The unserved wedge is narrow but real. (1) No product found in this session combines a binary, evidence-backed 'Readiness Ladder' for the last 90 days before RFS (utility energization letter, MV gear energization, Cx Level 4/5 and IST pass/fail counts, CDU flush and pressure tests, fiber acceptance, punch-list burn-down, OEM startup-tech availability) with a probabilistic RFS-by-date output and draw or covenant triggers. (2) Satellite and database vendors (SynMax, IIR, Currence, Epoch) cover the exterior and the announced schedule, and their materials do not claim commissioning or energization evidence. (3) GPU-deal technical advisors, as described by Peony, focus on fleet, telemetry and power documents rather than data hall commissioning. (4) Traditional IEs are slow, tied to a single lender or borrower, and priced for large project-finance deals. A fixed-fee, two-week, desk-plus-site 'second opinion' for a private credit desk, insurer or offtaker appears unserved. (5) The offtaker and backstop side (AI labs signing take-or-pay capacity, Google or Nvidia-style backstop providers) is structurally underserved because IEs work for lenders. Risks: incumbent IEs and Cx firms can add this as a service line, SemiAnalysis could bolt it on, and the business is people-bound (bench of ex-Cx leads) with limited software moat. Access to sites, contractors and Cx records depends on borrower cooperation, which means lender-imposed information covenants or offtaker leverage. || Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Ethyco (data center commissioning, warranty-phase support), Anyset AI (agentic closeout / warranty tracking), Nomic (AEC document AI, closeout), Trane delayed start-up warranty (OEM rider). White space: Nobody I found combines all of these for data center MEP: (1) a serial-number-level clock ledger built for idle or deferred-start halls, (2) a pre-expiry loaded stress test using the idle capacity, (3) OEM claim filing and start-date deferral negotiation, and (4) success-fee or fixed-fee pricing sold to the owner or its lender. The pieces exist separately. Anyset and Nomic do doc extraction. Ethyco-style Cx firms do a 10-month warranty review. Wind and solar have end-of-warranty inspection and claims firms. OEMs sell delayed-start riders. Load-bank vendors have the hardware. Data center power and cooling MEP has no dedicated end-of-warranty claims specialist that I could find. Three structural weaknesses limit the wedge. (a) The clocks mostly start at OEM startup, and startup plus IST with load banks already loads equipment in Cx, so the 'idle for 12+ months' exposure is narrower than the pitch implies. It mainly hits gear started early or shipped more than 18 months before use. (b) 'Recovered value' is really avoided repair cost. It is hard to measure and easy for OEMs to dispute, and OEMs can deny on storage or light-load grounds (wet stacking is explicitly excluded, https://cliffordpower.com/wet-stacking-why-its-important-to-load-bank-your-diesel-generator/). A pure 25-30% contingency model will be hard to collect. (c) Documents are the commodity step, so the moat has to be inspection plus OEM leverage, not the LLM pipeline.

title: Contingency Spread Recovery for Public Benefit Pools
one_liner: Zero-upfront PBM pass-through audits sold to school and local-government benefit pools, paid as a share of verified savings, using a shadow pharmacy price list built from local independents' remits, with a slice of each fee paid back to those pharmacies.
customer: Executive directors and boards of multi-employer public benefit pools: school-district benefit trusts and joint powers authorities, county-association and municipal-league health trusts, with 5,000-100,000 lives across dozens of member entities. They buy once for many districts, are subject to open-records and audit pressure, and carry political risk if a PBM overcharge surfaces. Secondary: single counties or districts of 300-3,000 lives (free pilot tier). Payer is the pool, only when savings are verified. No PBM ever pays us.
problem: A pool pays its PBM a billed price per NDC per claim, and its contract may promise pass-through, lowest-of pricing or audit rights. It cannot see what the PBM paid the pharmacy, so the audit rights only test billing against the PBM's own data. Consultants either charge flat fees on PBM-supplied files or are compensated in part by carriers and PBMs (disclosure of broker and consultant compensation is now required under the 2021 Consolidated Appropriations Act, though disclosure is not independence). Local officials also watch the town's last pharmacy close while the same PBM underpays it. The old obstacle was a claim-level join needing consent from both sides, which is why the parent's tie-out looked hard.
solution: (1) Shadow price list: 20-40 in-region independents contribute NDC-level paid unit price, fill date and BIN/PCN/group only (no patient identifiers), extracted locally. The team reconstructs, by week, what the PBM's retail network actually pays per NDC for the top 200-300 generics that drive most retail generic spend. (2) Tie-out to any plan: take the pool's own claims file (via contractual audit right or public-records request) and compare billed unit price per NDC and date to the reconstructed pharmacy-paid price, producing a spread per member per month by drug. The pharmacies never need to have filled that plan's claims, because a network's pharmacy MAC is common across clients. Scope is stated honestly as retail, and mail and specialty are excluded unless data exists. (3) Screen first: only take pools whose contracts promise pass-through or lowest-of pricing, or who will run an RFP; ordinary legal spread contracts yield renegotiation, not breach recovery. (4) Act: audit-rights letter, renegotiation, or an RFP among 3-5 bidders including the Big 3 and transparent PBMs. (5) Optional Local Access Rider: the pool redirects about 20% of verified savings into a per-Rx access fee paid to in-county independents, a plan-design choice that keeps pharmacies alive and makes them allies. Savings are verified by replaying 12 months post-change against the same shadow list, with a cap.
why_now: Local officials have political will after Rite Aid's exit and Walgreens' closures. Fiduciary and open-records pressure on PBM spend is rising, transparent PBMs give pools credible switch destinations, and federal and state reporting mandates create a paper trail to check (verify current scope). LLM and OCR parsing makes contributing remits a one-day task. January renewals also drive RFP timing, and pools' boards typically decide in Q4-Q1.
revenue_model: Contingency of 12-15% of first-year verified savings, with a floor for pools over 10,000 lives. Illustrative: a 20,000-life pool spends roughly $25-30M a year on drugs; a 4-8% price gap is $1-2M and a 12% share is $120-240k. Recurring Pass-Through Monitor after the audit at about $0.30-0.40 per member per month ($70-95k a year for 20,000 lives). Data co-op dividend: 15-20% of fees paid to contributing pharmacies pro rata as a fair-market-value data license (never tied to referrals; structure with counsel, and keep it away from any federal program business). A few hundred such pools nationally make this a $30M-100M revenue niche.
non_obvious_insight: The employer does not need the claims the pharmacies saw. A PBM's retail pharmacy price list is common across clients in a network tier, so a crowd of pharmacies can reconstruct the hidden list once and any plan's billed prices can be compared to it. That turns a two-party consent-and-join problem into a price-list problem, and each additional pool costs almost nothing to audit. Contingency plus zero PBM money creates the only auditor with clean hands in a field where advisors are paid by the counterparties. Public bodies can compel data that private employers cannot, and the Local Access Rider turns the pharmacies from data suppliers into political allies.
first_30_days: Pick one state with many independents and public pools. Days 1-10: recruit 20 pharmacies through the state association, offering a free margin report in exchange for NDC-level price extracts; build the shadow list for the top 200 generics. Days 10-25: offer one county or district (300-3,000 lives) a free pilot, obtain its claims file by consent or open-records request, and produce a one-page spread letter with a dollars-per-member figure. Days 20-30: take the letter to a pool's executive director and broker and negotiate a contingency letter agreement (12% of verified savings, no fee if zero). Hire a healthcare attorney for data-license and dividend terms. Kill criterion: the pilot shows under 2% spread on retail generics, or fewer than 12 pharmacies agree to contribute.
lineage: mutation of I1266 ('Pharmacy-Side PBM Ledger for Employers'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Truveris (truAudit / truGuard / Marketplace), Capital Rx (Judi Health), AffirmedRx, SmithRx. White space: Caveat on confidence: my WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted before I ran any query in this session. The verdict rests on direct fetches of about 20 competitor and source pages plus GitHub searches, not on a broad landscape scan. It is a provisional 'gap', not a confirmed one.

What I did not find: no company that ingests pharmacy-side remits, benchmarks per-drug, per-PBM reimbursement against a peer pool, models Q4 network offers, and ties pharmacy-paid amounts to an employer's PBM claims file. The employer-side audit market is served: Truveris, benefits consultants, and transparent PBMs that market pass-through. Their audits appear to start from what the PBM hands over, and I found no sign they hold the pharmacy-paid half.

The pharmacy-side gap is plausible. PioneerRx, PQS and CPESN pages show no reimbursement-benchmarking or contract-modeling feature. Not verified: pharmacy services administrative organizations (PSAOs such as Cardinal, AmerisourceBergen Elevate, AAP, Health Mart Atlas) and pharmacy management system vendors may already offer contract review or reimbursement reports to members. Confirm this in customer interviews before building, because the PSAOs negotiate PBM contracts and already hold members' remits.

The specific unserved wedge is a claim-level reconciliation between the pharmacy's actual paid amount and the employer's PBM claims file, delivered as a spread and rebate pass-through gap in dollars per member.

Risks that shrink the white space:
- PBM provider-manual confidentiality clauses and possible antitrust or information-exchange concerns when pooling competitors' reimbursement rates.
- Getting employer PBM claims files with sponsor consent.
- Pharmacy remits are not uniformly 835 files.
- The January 2027 contract window is roughly 3 months away and cannot be met by a product built from scratch. | How this version avoids them: Truveris and benefits consultants start from what the PBM hands over and charge fixed fees or carry PBM-linked compensation; this starts from the price the pharmacy was actually paid, is paid only on verified savings, and takes no PBM money. They are also possible channel partners for pools that already use them. Capital Rx, AffirmedRx and SmithRx are the bidders and landing spots the audit sends pools toward, and we take no referral fee from them, which keeps the audit credible; they also cannot verify their own pass-through claims without a third party's pharmacy data. rx-gap-finder is a pharmacy-only underwater-Rx flagger with no employer price side. PQS and CPESN are recruiting channels for pharmacies, not competitors. The target is public pools and counties, a segment the competitor research did not show any of them serving, but this is unverified and should be checked in interviews.

title: Pet Claims Clearinghouse Starting at the Front Desk
one_liner: Invert the parent: instead of insurers policing vet invoices after the fact, give vet clinics a carrier-agnostic estimate-to-payout tool at the counter, then grow it into the standard transaction layer for pet insurance and a same-day payment network.
customer: Practice managers and lead client-service staff at independent and small-group US general-practice clinics (2-8 vets), and emergency or specialty hospitals where tickets run above $1,500. There are about 28,000 US vet hospitals. Later payers are pet insurers (per clean claim) and financing partners (per referred loan).
problem: An owner stands at the counter with a $3,800 estimate and says 'I have insurance'. It is one of about 15 carriers, the front desk cannot tell what will be covered, and the owner declines, delays, goes on credit or, in the worst case, euthanizes. Survey data shows 85% of vet professionals see owners decline recommended care at $1,000 or less, and they estimate about 13% of euthanasia decisions are driven by cost. After treatment, staff spend up to 30 minutes per claim in each insurer's own portal. Trupanion's VetDirect Pay shows clinics adopt this when it removes paperwork and lets them quote net of insurance (about 11,500 clinics as of October 2025, and a Digitail integration in August 2026), but it works only for Trupanion pets. Trupanion holds roughly 12% share in the market estimates found, so most insured pets have no such tool.
solution: Wedge product (shippable in about 10 weeks). Estimate Check: the front desk uploads the estimate or PMS export and the owner's policy PDF or insurance card. The tool returns per-line 'likely covered, likely excluded, needs records', a projected reimbursement range, and a one-page owner sheet showing what they will likely pay today and after reimbursement, with a financing option for any gap. It also shows the parent's edit logic turned around as provider-side scrubber tips ('these five lines are usually treated as included in the surgical fee; quote as a package price'). Claim Pack: after treatment it assembles the canonical invoice, records and the insurer's form, sends it through that insurer's intake channel, and tracks status. Network path: every estimate and reimbursement outcome trains per-insurer payout predictions. A published open transaction set (estimate, eligibility, claim, remittance on VeNom-based codes) is offered to insurers, who adopt it to cut intake cost. Later, an instant advance to clinics on insurer remits, funded by a warehouse line, turns it into a balance-sheet payment network.
why_now: Direct-pay proved clinic demand, but it is fragmented by carrier: Digitail and Trupanion announced their integration only in August 2026, and each new PMS-insurer pair is a one-off build. Insured pets are growing about 9% a year on a 4.27% penetration base, so the share of clinic estimates touched by insurance keeps rising. LLMs can now read arbitrary policy PDFs and messy estimates, which is what previously made a multi-carrier tool uneconomic. Corporate consolidation and price inflation make estimate conversations harder every quarter.
revenue_model: Phase 1: $199 a month per clinic location, sold on saved staff hours and higher treatment-plan acceptance, with a first-month free trial. Phase 2: insurers pay $0.75-$1.50 per clean canonical claim (their manual intake cost, an assumption to test), and financing partners pay a referral fee on loans originated at the estimate moment. Phase 3: 1.5-2.5% on advanced remit dollars (assumed range). Illustrative year-5 scale: 3,000 clinics at $2.4k is about $7M, 5M claims at $1 is about $5M, and $1B of advanced remits at 2% is about $20M, so roughly $30M of revenue on about a quarter of an estimated $4B of US claims paid.
non_obvious_insight: In human health, most claim edits run on the provider side, in clearinghouse scrubbers, before submission. Edits create value when they change behavior before the service, not when they reduce a payment afterwards. In pet insurance the only party who can renegotiate an estimate is the vet at the counter, and the only party with a real incentive at that moment is the clinic, because declined treatment is lost revenue. Flipping the parent's edits to the provider side removes its central risk (balance bills without vet contracts) and makes the vet a voluntary distribution channel. Whoever owns the estimate screen owns the transaction standard, just as the claim form did in human health, and the standard is worth more than any single edit library.
first_30_days: Week 1-2: recruit an ex-practice-manager co-founder and sit with 10 clinics, shadowing 30 insured-estimate conversations. Collect 200 real estimates with matching policy documents and reimbursement outcomes from 5 friendly clinics. Week 2-3: build the line normalizer and coverage rules for the top 8 carriers from public policy forms. Week 3-4: run a manual-assist 'Estimate Check in 15 minutes' service for 10 clinics by text or email, free, and score predictions against actual reimbursements (target: within 10% of the actual payout on at least 70% of cases). Convert 5 clinics to $199 a month by day 30 and ask the two most engaged to introduce their PMS account manager, which starts the marketplace-app conversation.
lineage: mutation of I1056 ('Unbundling Edits for Pet Insurance Claims'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: VetControl (Illingen, Germany), Five Sigma (Clive AI claims adjuster), Sirma (custom ML for PetsBest, now under Synchrony), FairVet. White space: Nobody I found sells a US, insurer-facing, explainable edit library (canonical line-item codes, bundling and duplicate rules, unit plausibility, reason codes) with cross-carrier benchmarks, to mid-size MGAs and TPAs.

- VetControl is the only true direct analog, and it is German, GOT-based, a services-plus-software hybrid, and shows no US customers.
- Five Sigma and Sirma classify line items for coverage, not for pricing or bundling.
- FairVet and Vet Receipt hold consumer-sourced benchmark data with no insurer-grade normalization.
- Trupanion and Lassie built in-house and are not customers.
- Verisk has standardized the policy side only.

The unserved gap is an invoice-derived, ZIP-level, procedure-level price index built from insurer claims, which no owner-upload app can match in volume. It would be joined to explainable pay/reduce/review decisions for mid-size carriers with no data science team.

Structural risk to flag. Human-health edits work because of provider contracts and CMS rules. Pet insurers have no contracts with vets and no 'global fee' concept, and they pay owners by reimbursement. Line-level reductions therefore land on policyholders as balance bills, which invites complaints and regulatory attention. I found no US insurer RFP or public spend for this. The demand evidence is indirect: cost inflation, plus vendors like VetControl selling a similar product in Germany. | How this version avoids them: Trupanion VetDirect Pay is single-carrier and proprietary, and it locks in Trupanion pets, so it cannot be the neutral rail, and the roughly 88% of the market outside its share is untouched by it. Insurer-specific direct-pay programs (Pets Best, ASPCA, Healthy Paws, PumpkinNow) each require a separate clinic workflow. PMS vendors (Digitail, Covetrus, IDEXX and others) integrate one insurer at a time, lack the insurer-side coverage logic, and are channel partners here rather than rivals. Five Sigma, Sirma, VetControl and Lassie sit on the insurer side and never see the estimate. FairVet and Vet Receipt are consumer after-the-fact bill checkers with no payout logic. Verisk standardized policy forms, not transactions. General eligibility-verification vendors (DoctorConnect lists pet insurers among its payers) are appointment and human-health tools without line-level pet estimates or claim packaging. I could not verify their depth, so that is a risk to test in the first 30 days. Moving the edits to the provider side also sidesteps the balance-bill and regulatory pushback the parent's research flagged.

title: Keep-Warm: Preserving Power in Idle Plants
one_liner: Invert the database: instead of scoring dead plants once, sell a monthly service that keeps their electrical service alive and monitored, then turn 200 preserved shells into a right-of-first-offer inventory and, later, a balance-sheet powered-shell bank.
customer: Wedge: banks, special servicers and lenders holding real-estate-owned industrial plants, plus corporate owners of mothballed plants and county land banks, in the Mahoning Valley and Akron/Canton first. Later buyers: data-center, battery and manufacturing developers who pay for shells certified 'energized-ready'.
problem: An idle plant's electrical system is a wasting asset on a clock. Standard commercial property policies limit cover for vandalism, theft, water damage and sprinkler leakage once a building has been vacant for about 60 days (an assumption to verify with an insurance broker), copper theft and roof leaks wreck switchgear, utilities can pull service or reclassify accounts on idle meters, oil-filled transformers degrade, and permit fees and reports lapse. Residential-style property-preservation firms winterize and change locks, but nobody is paid to preserve amps. Owners find out the plant is worth far less than it was only when a buyer's electrician opens the gear two years later.
solution: Two tiers. 'Watch' at $650 per month: baseline electrician record (the Power Passport becomes the set-up fee), a $600 sensor kit (humidity, temperature, door, current clamps on the main service, cellular camera), quarterly thermography, and an insurer-facing monthly report. 'Warm' at $2,200 per month: monthly electrician visits, keep-energized management with the utility including minimum-bill and account status, annual transformer oil sampling, dehumidification, theft-alarm response and permit fee and report compliance. The continuous data produces an 'energized-ready' score, days to first power, and a verified time series no one-off inspection can match. Marketing and right-of-first-offer rights are bundled into the contract for owners who want a sale.
why_now: Low-cost cellular sensors and cameras collapsed to tens of dollars a unit. Vision models now read nameplates and gear photos cheaply, which cuts analyst hours per building. More industrial shells are going idle while buyers now pay a premium for existing power, so, for the first time, preserving the electrical system has a positive return.
revenue_model: Recurring: $650 or $2,200 per building per month plus a $2,500 baseline record; a carry-cost comparison shows a 300k sq ft idle plant costing an owner roughly $15k-$40k per month, so the service is 3-8% on top of existing carry. Gross margin about 50-55% at 10 buildings per electrician route. Insurer angle: partner with a vacant-property insurance managing general agent to turn monitoring into a rating credit, which can pay for itself. Scale path: 200 buildings on Warm and Watch is about $4M-$5M annual recurring revenue; the contract's right of first offer gives inventory to sell to buyers on a fee basis; a later fund of $50M-$100M exercises options on the best 20 shells, subdivides them into permitted 'factory condos' or powered shells and sells or leases at a premium. First 6 months: 5-8 paying buildings.
non_obvious_insight: The same service that stops the asset dying also builds the only dataset that matters: a time series of load, temperature, humidity and access on hundreds of idle industrial buildings, and exclusive access to a pipeline of them. That combination is a cornered resource plus a switching cost, defended by contracts and data history and not by scoring algorithms anyone can copy. The parent is a snapshot; this is the movie, and a monthly bill is a better business than a report.
first_30_days: Week 1: list 40 idle plants owned by banks, special servicers and land banks from county auditor and REO data in two metros; contact 8 REO and asset managers. Week 2: call two vacant-property insurance brokers and one managing general agent to test whether monitoring earns a premium credit or a vacancy-clause endorsement (the riskiest assumption). Weeks 3-4: sign three 90-day pilots on Watch at a waived set-up fee in exchange for a case study and marketing rights, install kits, and deliver the first insurer-facing report. Success test: one lender converts to $650 per month paid and one insurer or broker confirms a written premium credit or vacancy accommodation.
lineage: mutation of I0820 ('Power Passport: Scoring Dead Factories on Amps, Permits'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Brownfield.ai, Scout (ScoutCities), LandGate, Enverus Site & Screen. White space: Nobody I found productises a building-level, physically verified 'inside-the-fence' record for dead Midwest plants. That record would cover the electrician-verified main service size, voltage, gear age and nameplates, spare capacity, slab and crane-rail condition, the state of the existing air and wastewater permits, and a utility will-serve letter, all in a scored, comparable format sold before the deal. The funded players (LandGate, Enverus, GridCARE, Paces) work at the substation and grid level and are aimed at data centers. Utility and state databases (JobsOhio, AEP, FirstEnergy, ZoomProspector) verify sites and utility service, not building gear or permit status. Scout and Brownfield.ai are the closest competitors, but they look desktop- and network-led with no per-building inspection, and I found no evidence they carry electrician-verified data. The genuine gap is a trusted, standardised, seller-commissioned building electrical and permit record, not the parcel-scoring layer, which is already crowded and funded. The idea's weaker points: the Ohio permit-transferability wedge is thin (see evidence), and it is unproven that brokers will pay $1.5k-$3.5k. | How this version avoids them: None of the parent's competitors monitor or preserve anything. Brownfield.ai, Scout, LandGate, Enverus, GridCARE, Paces and ZoomProspector sell data or listings, and JobsOhio and the utility databases are free lists. PCA and electrical inspection firms sell a one-time report, and residential property-preservation and big facilities-management firms cover occupied, high-value assets or locks and lawns, not energized-capacity preservation. The business is recurring service revenue with a proprietary time series, so a funded data competitor would have to hire electricians and sign owner contracts to copy it, and the exclusive marketing rights become a cornered resource.

title: Solos Refer, We File: National Delay-Suit Bench
one_liner: Invert the tool model: a lawyer-owned litigation bench that takes stuck cases referred by immigration solos, files at industrial speed for about 60% of the boutique price, and pays the referring lawyer a fee share, building a national referral network and the full-cycle dataset as a by-product.
customer: Payer: stuck applicants (post-interview N-400, I-751, I-765, long-idle I-130/I-140) referred by their own immigration lawyer, paying a $2,995 flat fee plus about $455 in costs. Channel: 1-10 attorney immigration firms in NY, NJ and CT that hold stuck clients but will not be counsel of record on a federal suit. Expansion: solos in any state, then boutique firms as overflow customers.
problem: The parent's model needs solos to pay $400 to do something they fear, and the research found no evidence that solos pay for tooling. What solos do have is client trust and a pile of stuck files. Their current choices are to do nothing or to refer the client to a boutique for no reward and the risk of losing the client. Meanwhile the one visible provider (Mandamus.com) is a small boutique with about 30 litigated petitions in 15 years, prices at $5,000 plus $500, and runs no co-counsel program for other lawyers. That leaves a large pool of unserved clients who cannot pay $5,000.
solution: A lawyer-owned litigation bench with the software company as management-services provider under a flat per-case fee (not a percentage of legal fees). The referral flow: a solo submits a stuck case through a 4-minute referral link or a case-management export; the ledger triages it (declining nationality-hold suits and Fifth Circuit I-485 claims); the client e-signs a fee-division consent that names each lawyer's share and the joint responsibility; the bench files within 72 hours, runs the 60-day clock, negotiates consent-order-first, and files the EAJA petition when a consent order supports it. The referring lawyer stays counsel on the underlying application, receives status in their own system, and earns 30% ($900) of the fee. The flat fee covers all litigation including an MTD opposition, matching the boutique's promise. Key legal gate: joint-responsibility fee division rules vary by state (NY 1.5(g) and ABA Model Rule 1.5(e) style), so launch only where ethics counsel clears it.
why_now: AI drafting and docket automation cut attorney time per routine filing from 6-10 hours to about 3 with paralegal support, which lets price fall to roughly 60% of the boutique at a healthy margin. The USAO's 45-90 day resolution pattern means one litigator can carry 60-100 live files, so the constraint on a litigation shop is intake, not lawyer time. Solos are overloaded and fear being first to file. The research found no co-counsel or referral program for other lawyers, so the economics of referral are unexploited.
revenue_model: Client pays $2,995 flat (court costs about $455 passed through). Referral share $900. Illustrative unit economics (assumptions): about $300 paralegal and attorney time, $40 service, about $225 expected tail (15% of cases x roughly $1,500 of MTD opposition work), $60 support, leaving about $1,450 contribution per case. 3,000 cases a year (a year-3 target that requires expanding the market, since the RECAP sample shows only 350-480 filings a year) would produce about $4.3M contribution. Upside: license the ledger, sell overflow capacity to boutiques, and reuse the same referral rails for other agency-delay claims (consular administrative processing, FOIA, passports).
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is not tooling but willingness to be counsel of record. Solos already own client trust and stuck files but earn nothing from referring out and fear the suit; a fee share for zero litigation risk turns them from prospects who must be persuaded to pay into an eager, unpaid-acquisition channel, at 30% of fee versus the boutique's SEO and ad spend. Because most cases moot in weeks, the bench recycles capacity fast, and it is the bench, not a tool, that naturally accumulates the full-cycle data (service date, USCIS action date, fee outcome) that makes the ledger better than anyone's public docket analytics. Scale economies and a referral network are both reachable within 24 months.

Conn. (the Mandamus.com boutique, admitted in D. Conn., D.D.C. and S.D. Tex., is a possible bench partner rather than only a rival); draft the referral agreement and client consent. Days 10-30: recruit 15 NY/NJ/CT solos through AILA chapters and direct outreach to attorneys of record on RECAP naturalization suits, pre-load 30 stuck cases from their own books, file the first 10 within 72 hours of consent, log every outcome, and pay the first referral share when the client pays. Go/no-go: 10 cases filed, more than half of referrers sending a second case, and modeled contribution of at least $1,000 per case.

title: Lender-Required Curtailment Reports for Data Centers
one_liner: An independent, productized report, like a Phase I environmental report but for power, that tells data center lenders how many hours a campus can legally run its generators when the grid curtails it.
customer: Debt originators, underwriters and portfolio managers who finance data centers where the lender carries power risk directly: neocloud GPU-backed delayed-draw loans, spec and powered-land developers without an investment-grade tenant, and ABS/CMBS arrangers and rating analysts. The borrower pays at closing, as it already does for lender-required third-party reports. Independent engineers and lender counsel are the channel. Start with PJM and ERCOT campuses.
problem: Every underwriting model assumes that if PJM or ERCOT curtails the campus, the on-site generators cover it. Federal engine rules and state air permits cap those engines at roughly 100 hours a year, with at most 50 for non-emergency use, and none of it can be run for money or under a financial arrangement. Texas SB 6 even states that it does not authorize violating emissions limits. A campus curtailed for 200 hours can be legally uncovered after 100. Lenders have no independent way to check this. The operator's own consultant is conflicted, and independent engineers are generalists. The exposure is real but unquantified, and it will be priced once someone quantifies it.
solution: A standardized 'Curtailment Runway Report', delivered in about five business days. It has four parts. (1) The permit-derived legal runway: per-engine hour caps, engine tier, allowed uses, monitoring and reporting duties, and remaining headroom. (2) Operational runway: fuel on site, paralleling and telemetry status, and the test and maintenance hours already consumed. (3) A curtailment-exposure distribution for the campus's utility and market zone. (4) A cost-to-cure estimate (permit modification, SCR, hour cap changes). Every report cites the permit conditions it relies on and is reviewed by a retained air attorney. A portfolio subscription adds permit-change alerts and annual surveillance refreshes. Campuses that score badly become inbound leads for the sharpened dual-mode permit service.
why_now: PJM's July 2026 auction was 6.8 GW short and its board plan lets large loads bring their own capacity or accept earlier curtailment. The curtailment rules are now credit terms rather than a policy debate. Texas SB 6 requires 75 MW+ loads to disclose backup generation and lets ERCOT direct deployment, so disclosure data will exist for the first time. Data center financing volume is large and recurring, and power availability is now the top diligence item. LLM-assisted structuring of permit PDFs collapses the cost of producing a first-draft report, while attorney review keeps it defensible.
revenue_model: $20-45k per closing report, paid by the borrower through the lender's third-party report budget. Annual surveillance refresh at $8-12k per campus. Lender or rating-agency portfolio subscriptions at $150-400k a year for unlimited reports and change alerts. Illustrative sizing to validate: 150 financings a year x $30k, plus 400 refreshes x $8k, plus 10 subscriptions x $250k, is roughly $10M annual revenue. Gross margin is high once permits are structured, because the same permit dataset serves every report. A white-label channel to independent engineers is a second line.
non_obvious_insight: The parent's permit dataset is worth more as a warning than as an unlock. Everyone else asks how much diesel can become capacity. The same facts show that the fallback everyone already assumes is often illegal past the cap, which is a downside risk with a faster buyer and no retrofit capex. Lenders reliably pay for independent third-party reports that gate a closing (Phase I environmental reports are the analogy, and the database company behind them proved the data business). Independence is the product. The operator's consultant cannot sell the same report, and aggregators profit from enrollment and have no incentive to say 'no'. A bad score also creates the demand the unlock business could never verify.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: build 10 sample reports on publicly permitted PJM and ERCOT campuses using permit files and disclosure data, and retain an air attorney to co-sign the methodology. Days 5-25: interview 15 people, namely data center debt originators, private credit underwriters, ABS/CMBS rating analysts, lender counsel and independent engineers, to find who owns power diligence in credit committee and which live deals are closing in the next 90 days. Days 20-30: offer three free reports on live deals in exchange for a 30-minute review and permission to cite, then price the fourth at $25k. Get one independent-engineer white-label LOI. The riskiest assumption is that a lender will make this a closing condition. Test it by asking for the condition in writing.

competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Voltus, CPower, Enchanted Rock (ERock), Trinity Consultants (data center and power team). White space: Verification caveat: the session's WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted, so no search-engine, Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or TechCrunch queries could be run. I did about 30 direct page fetches and 2 GitHub searches instead. The GitHub searches found no open-source tool for this. I found no company selling a fixed-price 'permit-to-dispatch' package for existing data center diesel fleets (permit modification, emissions retrofit financing, telemetry, PJM enrollment and M&V). That is absence of evidence from a constrained search, not proof that none exists.

What appears unserved:
(1) A productized, per-state permit playbook tied to capacity outcomes. Trinity-type consultants sell hourly, per-project permitting. DR aggregators (Voltus, CPower) sell enrollment and revenue share. Generator OEMs and ERock sell hardware. Nobody I found owns the seam between them.
(2) Retrofit financing on the subset of engines that need it.
(3) A permit-headroom dataset across Title V and minor-source files.

The binding constraint is legal, not competitive. Under 40 CFR 63.6640(f), as summarized from Cornell LII, emergency engines are limited to 100 hours a year for maintenance, testing and emergencies, with at most 50 of those for non-emergency use. The 50 hours cannot be used for peak shaving or non-emergency demand response, and cannot generate income or serve a financial arrangement with another entity. Only narrow exceptions exist, dispatched by local authorities for transmission and distribution limits. Selling emergency-designated diesel as PJM capacity therefore likely requires reclassifying engines as non-emergency, which triggers stricter engine standards (Tier 4 or SCR-type controls), plus state NOx limits and possible major-source permitting. That is why the founder's 'retrofit the subset' step is likely the real cost and risk. It is also why incumbents have stayed away. The wedge exists only where the permit and retrofit math actually closes.

Other risks: PJM DR accreditation rules and limited-duration derating, which I could not verify because the PJM manual fetch returned only a table of contents. Local opposition to diesel. Hyperscalers and utilities choosing gas or battery capacity instead. | How this version avoids them: Voltus, CPower and ERock are sellers of megawatts, so they have no incentive to tell a lender a campus is uncovered, and none serves the capital-markets buyer. Trinity works for the operator, which is a conflict in a lender report, and it sells hourly permit projects rather than a standardized, comparable score. Independent engineers are the likely adjacent entrants. We sell to them white-label and win on speed, a permit-structured dataset and a lawyer-reviewed methodology. No competitor found in the parent's research sells to lenders, insurers or rating analysts.

title: Escrow and Assay Settlement House for Scrap
one_liner: A neutral settlement house that holds the buyer's money in a licensed escrow and the sealed sample in a vault, then releases payment automatically on the assay of record. It starts with black mass and grows into a registry, financing and an index.
customer: Two sides. Sellers are mid-size dismantlers and pre-processors who fear both assay games and recycler insolvency after the 2025 restructurings. Buyers are recyclers who want to win feed, especially weakly capitalised or new-capacity ones that can rent credibility from a neutral escrow. The first anchor is one buyer signing our Standard Settlement Terms, which opens every one of its sellers at once. A buyer pays half the fee.
problem: The parent sells arbitration after the fight, once, to a price-sensitive party in trouble. Sellers actually face two bundled anxieties on every lot. One is assay noise or bias. The other is credit exposure on the assay-based final payment, unsecured for weeks and frozen if the lot is disputed. After Li-Cycle's sale to Glencore and other 2025 restructurings, sellers price that risk by discounting or refusing weaker buyers. Nobody sells both fixes in one contract. Banks' letters of credit and provisional payments cover part of the credit side, and assay disputes are left to umpire clauses.
solution: Sold within six months as a Settle-in-14-days contract pack. It is a tri-party agreement (buyer, seller, us) drafted once by a trade-finance law firm. A licensed escrow agent or bank partner holds funds, and we never hold money or inventory. A certified crew takes a sealed triplicate sample-of-record at the seller's dock. One split goes to a pre-agreed accredited lab, and two are stored in a third-party vault. Payment releases by formula, payable times assay-of-record, with no ex-post negotiation. Only if the retained splits differ beyond the pre-agreed Gy variance tolerance is the third split assayed. Later layers are these. (1) An accreditation programme so inspection companies' and recyclers' crews sample under our protocol and pay a licence, so the majors distribute us. (2) A lot registry whose receipts lenders advance 85-90% against, for an origination share. (3) An assay-consistent payables index sold to price reporting agencies. (4) Extension to e-scrap boards, catalyst scrap, mixed copper and Ni/Co intermediates.
why_now: Counterparty fear is at a high after the 2025 restructurings, and buyers need a way to attract supply. Black mass flows are being channelled into a bounded, regulated EU/OECD corridor, so a few dozen counterparties and a few hundred lanes can be covered by one house. Escrow and instant-payment rails, e-signature and vault-and-hash registries are now commodity. Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/606 already forces lot-level composition records that the registry can generate.
revenue_model: A take rate of 0.8-1.2% of lot value split between buyer and seller (EUR 1-1.8k on a EUR 150k lot). A pass-through crew fee of EUR 600-900. Small float income. A 0.3-0.5% lender origination share once receipts are financeable. Accreditation licences. Bottom-up: if European black mass trades EUR 0.5-1.5B a year (an estimate, unverified), 1% on a third of it is EUR 2-5M a year before scrap classes beyond black mass. The scale story is the registry and standard, with the lender and index revenue on top. It is a settlement network with float, not a lab.
non_obvious_insight: Inversion: buyers and sellers do not need a smarter referee, they need the decision made before the dispute. Moving the assay of record from ex-post arbitration to an ex-ante release trigger converts a service sold once, in trouble, into infrastructure sold on every lot with a take on GMV. The most credit-challenged recycler is the natural first buyer, because a neutral escrow lets it rent credibility, so the expected resistor is the first to sign. Independence stays the asset, because only a party that neither samples for a side nor holds inventory can be the registry.
first_30_days: Draft the tri-party terms with a trade-finance law firm (about EUR 8-15k) and shortlist two escrow or bank partners. Pitch five recyclers, prioritising new capacity or weak balance sheets, on being the anchor buyer for Standard Settlement Terms. Pitch the three sellers from the audit funnel. Target one signed letter of intent from a buyer and three escrowed lots at half fee by month 4. Check whether digital metals trading platforms such as Metalshub already run escrow plus assay for black mass, which I could not verify. Also test with one lender whether a certified lot receipt would raise their advance rate.

title: Store Takeover Truth Sheets for Lenders
one_liner: Buyers and lenders of Japanese convenience-store franchise takeovers pay per deal for an independent contract-aware valuation sheet that shows the store's profit after replacing the owner's own labor, under that store's actual royalty and disposal-share terms, plus the ordering upside a new operator could capture.
customer: The payer is the acquirer and its lender, not the incumbent owner. First targets are Kansai multi-store franchise corporations buying additional stores, first-time entrants and second-career buyers taking over a store, and the loan officers at regional banks, shinkin banks and Japan Finance Corporation branches financing them, reached through the founder's own lender and succession advisors. The seller supplies the documents because the sale depends on it.
problem: A store is priced off the HQ-issued statement of 'owner income', which blends profit with wages for unpaid owner and family labor (often 80 to 100 hours a week each) and hides how contract terms bite. At Osaka's 1,231 yen minimum wage, a couple working 140 combined hours a week is worth roughly 9M yen a year before any night premium or manager overhead, so a store showing 10M yen of owner income may earn about 1M yen for a buyer who must hire. A legacy 15/85 disposal contract also hands the buyer 85% of waste risk, while the seller's waste partly reflects HQ-pushed ordering the buyer can change. With Seven's 2027 new contract (50/50, lower charge) never converting existing stores, buyers must now choose between a legacy store and opening a new one on better terms. HQ approves transferees and earns royalties from whoever operates, so it is not a neutral source. Nobody independent computes either adjustment, and this removes the retaliation fear that makes existing owners hard customers.
solution: An 8-page Store Truth Sheet produced in about 5 business days from seller documents (12 months of HQ monthly statements, disposal totals, hourly sales, labor rosters, the franchise agreement). It shows (1) reported owner income restated as profit after paying market-wage replacement labor at current and scheduled minimum wages, (2) royalty tier and disposal-share mechanics for that specific contract, with sensitivity to wage and sales changes, (3) a range for ordering and markdown upside under the new owner's own payoff (the owner-side newsvendor model), (4) remaining term, transfer and renewal-risk flags, and (5) a legacy versus new-store comparison for buyers who could open a fresh store instead. Lenders get a white-label credit-memo version and a 12-month covenant-monitoring option. Later, buyers who close the deal are the natural first customers for the ordering product.
why_now: Three shocks landed together: the 1 Oct 2026 wage step in Osaka, Diamond's report of a Seven internal simulation showing franchisee profit falling to about a third under wage increases, and Seven's June 2026 announcement of a 50/50 contract from autumn 2027 for new stores only. That last one splits the market into legacy and new-contract stores and makes the price of a legacy store genuinely uncertain. Extracting numbers from photographed Japanese statements is now cheap, cutting a manual diligence review that would otherwise be a multi-week accountant job. The store-takeover market is assumed to be growing with owner aging, which needs to be verified before scaling.
revenue_model: 180,000 yen per store diligence sheet paid by the buyer (120,000 yen each when a buyer takes 3 or more stores). Banks that make the sheet a loan condition pay 40,000 yen per file or a per-branch annual license, and can pass it to the borrower. Covenant monitoring at 3,000 yen per store per month for lenders holding loans. Succession advisors who refer deals earn a 10% referral fee. At 10 deals a month this is about 1.8M yen a month, and every sheet adds a contract-parameterized store record to a proprietary benchmark.
non_obvious_insight: The same document set produces two adjustments that point in opposite directions and are both invisible to buyer and seller: owner income falls once labor is priced, and waste upside rises once a new owner uses his own payoff instead of HQ's. Both sides currently negotiate on the HQ statement, so the party with the correct pair of numbers can price a deal better than either side, and a lender will pay for that. Because the buyer pays and has no HQ contract yet, the product sidesteps the fear of OFC retaliation and the franchise-agreement third-party data question is limited to seller-provided records in a sale process. The by-product is a growing cross-store dataset of real royalty, waste and labor economics that nobody outside HQ holds.
first_30_days: Days 1-5: produce Truth Sheets for the founder's own three stores and note the gap between reported income and after-replacement-labor profit. Days 3-10: ask the founder's own lender for a warm introduction to 5 loan officers and reach 3 to 5 succession advisors and multi-store corporations. Publish a free 'profit after replacing yourself' calculator with 6 inputs as the lead magnet. Days 10-30: run 2 free sheets on live deals in exchange for a case study and lender feedback, then sell 3 paid sheets at 180,000 yen (540,000 yen) with a money-back guarantee if the buyer does not find it useful. Kill signal: no live takeover deals found among 15 conversations, in which case the segment volume assumption is false. Also verify seller and HQ data-sharing terms with a franchise lawyer.
lineage: mutation of I0272 ('Owner-Side Ordering: The Royalty Asymmetry Calculator'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Seven-Eleven Japan AI ordering plus HQ-led markdown (Eco da Ne), Lawson AI.CO (ordering plus AI markdown recommendation), FamilyMart AI Recommend Ordering, Sinops (sinops-CLOUD AI markdown) with Sato. White space: No product found that is an independent owner-side payoff engine for Japanese convenience-store franchisees. Searches in Japanese and English returned no startup, SaaS or app that (a) uses the owner's actual royalty tier and disposal-share contract terms to compute order levels, (b) sets markdown timing from the owner's payoff, or (c) audits HQ AI recommendations against the owner's interest. Sinops, Wasteless, Afresh and Shelf Engine sell operations software to retailers and none values a franchise store. Too Good To Go is a surplus outlet. The union and ex-OFC consultants coach owners on markdowns with no calculators and do not sit on the buy side. title: Lender-Paid Calf Collateral Inspection and Lot Grading
one_liner: Sell independent day-3-to-6 lot grading to the feed, milk-replacer and ag-loan credit desks that finance calf raisers, as collateral inspection, so the party who really loses money on every dead calf pays for the measurement.
customer: Credit managers at regional feed and milk-replacer distributors that carry 30-90 day trade credit to calf ranches, and ag lenders and calf-ownership financing programs that lend against calf inventory. Wedge: one distributor with 15-40 non-integrated calf-raiser accounts and $2M or more in calf-related receivables. Raisers are the secondary beneficiary and pay through a loan-document inspection fee or through better credit terms.
problem: A 500-head lot of crossbred calves is now $500-750K of collateral, and the lender's monitoring is still a headcount and the raiser's own say-so. A bad intake lot with poor passive transfer can lose a large share of its calves within weeks (the parent's 10-25% raiser loss is unverified). My inference, to be validated in customer calls, is that the credit desk usually learns of it from a missed payment 30-60 days later. The lender cannot trust the raiser's self-reported Brix, and the raiser cannot prove to the lender that a bad lot was bad luck at intake rather than bad management. Nobody prices the biological quality of the collateral.
solution: For each new lot placed at a financed ranch, an independent tech samples 20 calves within 24-72 hours of arrival (day 3-6 of age), with custody-stamped tube and tag capture. Within 24 hours the credit desk receives a Lot Risk Grade (A-D) built from the Lombard tiers, with an expected 30-day loss band, taken from the published roughly 2x risk for failure of passive transfer at first and replaced by our own pooled data. Credit terms key off the grade: A lots get full limit and fast approval, C/D lots trigger a hold or a risk-sharing plan. The raiser gets a same-day early-warning call for D lots (isolate Poor calves, fluid and treatment protocol), so the inspection is a service to them rather than a tax. Year 2: a loss-outcome dataset licensed to reinsurers and MGAs.
why_now: Crossbred calf collateral per head has multiplied several times over versus a few years ago (beef-on-dairy went from about 50,000 head in 2014 to about 3.2M in 2024 per the parent, and calves have reached $1,500), so headcount-style monitoring that was fine at $100 a calf is negligent at $1,400. Cheap refractometers, phone custody capture and now a published grading standard make lot inspection cost about $1.50-2 a calf. The 2020 consensus tiers give lenders a common language for the first time.
revenue_model: $250-450 per lot inspected (about $1.50-2 per calf), billed to the lender or supplier and recoverable from the raiser as a collateral inspection fee, plus $150-300 a month per financed ranch for the monitoring dashboard. A ranch placing 300 calves a week is about 52 lots a year, or roughly $18K a year. A distributor with 40 accounts is about $700K a year. Later: loss-data license to insurers and reinsurers, and a per-lot fee for a lender-requested claims audit. Market ceiling on fees is modest but recurring, and the buyer's value (bad debt avoided) is a multiple of the fee.
non_obvious_insight: The party with the most money at risk per dead calf is not in the room and is not the raiser. It is the credit provider. Collateral management (independent inspectors working for banks) is an old, boring industry that has never priced the biological quality of livestock. This makes the business independent of two weaknesses in the parent: it needs no buyer premium for graded calves, and it avoids warranty moral hazard because the customer prices and monitors credit rather than insuring loss.
first_30_days: Days 1-14: hold 20 short calls with credit managers at feed and milk-replacer distributors and ag loan officers in one dairy-dense county. Ask what they lose per year to calf-ranch defaults, how they learn of a bad lot, and whether collateral inspection fees are already collectible under their loan documents. Days 15-30: sign a free 60-day pilot with one distributor covering 6 friendly ranches. Two techs, about 12 lots a week, and a 24-hour grade report the credit manager marks up with what they would have changed. At day 60, compare grade against 30-day loss and any past-due behavior, then ask for a signed $300-a-lot agreement. Gate: the credit manager names annual avoided bad debt of at least 10x the annual fee. If lenders will not state a number, kill it. Before pitching, verify the loss-rate and market-size figures and check for existing livestock collateral inspection firms.
lineage: mutation of I0617 ('Immune-Graded Beef-on-Dairy Calves With Warranty'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Where Food Comes From (third-party verification: Age Verification, Source Verification, USDA Process Verified Program, custom Process Verified claims), Calftech Corporation (Central Valley, CA calf ranch). White space: Coverage caveat: the WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was already spent when I started, so I could not run the planned searches on Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt, TechCrunch or vendor names. The 'nobody does this' finding therefore rests on direct page fetches and a GitHub repository search, not full web coverage. My early attempts to pull search-engine result pages through WebFetch returned junk or CAPTCHAs, and I stopped them because they sidestep the search limit. The verdict is low-to-moderate confidence.

What I found:
- No company selling per-calf independent Brix or serum total protein grading with a QR passport, and no calf-immunity warranty product. Where Food Comes From has no such program. Vytelle's site lists no calf program. GitHub has no relevant open-source tool, only hobby repos.
- Livestock Risk Protection explicitly 'does not protect against mortality, condemnation, physical damage or disease' (https://agproud.com/articles/60060-knowledge-is-the-best-insurance-an-overview-of-livestock-risk-protection). Federal cover for calf death loss is therefore absent. I did not verify what private mortality insurance exists.

What still stands in the way, and is not competition in the strict sense:
1. Self-testing. A raiser can Brix-test at arrival for about $1, and dairies can test their own calves. Independent custody only earns money where seller and buyer distrust each other's numbers, or where price is set before arrival.
2. Bilateral history. Feeders already ask which dairy the calves came from and some supply sire straws to dairies (https://agproud.com/articles/53106-factors-to-consider-before-buying-crossbred-dairy-beef-calves). Source-dairy reputation substitutes for per-calf grading.
3. Warranty moral hazard. Immunity is one driver of loss, but raiser housing, feeding and biosecurity dominate, which makes underwriting hard. Lombard's consensus paper puts failure of passive transfer at roughly twice the risk, which is a useful signal but not a full loss model.
4. Incumbents can absorb it. Verifiers, diagnostics vendors, calf-ranch networks and packer programs could add an immunity field.

Genuinely unserved: an independent, per-calf immunity record that travels from dairy to raiser to feeder to packer, plus a neutral dispute-resolution measurement. | How this version avoids them: Where Food Comes From sells claim verification to marketers, brands and packers. It has no lender product and does no per-lot sampling for credit decisions, so the buyer and the job are different. Calftech-style integrated ranches self-fund and self-monitor, so they are out of scope by design. This targets non-integrated raisers who have to prove intake quality to a lender, and independence is what makes an inspection valid collateral evidence. The $1 self-test objection disappears, because the lender is exactly the party who cannot accept the raiser's own test. There is no dependence on a graded-calf premium (the parent's weakest evidence) and no underwriting exposure. Vets who already test at herd checks work for the raiser and cannot serve as the lender's independent eyes.

title: Rural Vet Call Logs as Outbreak Early Warning
one_liner: Producers call the vet before they call the state. Anonymized weekly counts of abortions, maggot wounds, sudden deaths and respiratory clusters are a leading indicator that traders, insurers and packers will pay for.
customer: Buyers: cattle and feeder analytics desks, market advisory and commodity funds, packer and feedlot risk managers, livestock and dairy insurers or reinsurers, animal health company territory teams, and state animal health boards (contracts or grants). Suppliers are participating rural vets, who get free early regional alerts and a small revenue share.
problem: Official disease data lags by weeks because it waits on lab confirmation, and ranchers hesitate to report to the state because a quarantine costs them money. Screwworm was confirmed in a Texas calf in June 2026 after roughly 60 years without a US case, and H5N1 in dairy cattle was spreading for months before detection in 2024. Cattle futures at record prices with a 70-year low herd move violently on rumor, and nobody has a systematic ground-level feed.
solution: A 30-second end-of-week SMS or one-tap tally where each vet reports counts by syndrome (abortion clusters, navel or wound maggots, sudden deaths, neurological, respiratory, milk drops) and ZIP3 or county. Counts are aggregated with k-anonymity (no client identity, minimum practice thresholds) and compared to seasonal baselines. Outputs are a weekly 'Rural Vet Pulse' regional index, push alerts when a region deviates, and an API for institutional subscribers. Vets get the regional alerts free, which is the give-to-get hook.
why_now: New World screwworm has been confirmed in Texas and New Mexico since June 2026, with the first infested horse reported in September 2026, and movement restrictions plus sterile-fly shortages make the outbreak's trajectory the biggest driver of cattle risk. H5N1 in dairy is ongoing, federal animal health staffing is stretched, and academic syndromic surveillance systems exist in Europe (Netherlands, France, Great Britain) but I found no commercial equivalent built from US rural vet practices.
revenue_model: $2-10K per month per institutional data subscriber (analytics desks, insurers, packers), enterprise API tiers, sponsored regional alerts from animal health companies, state or regional government pilots, and a $100-300 per month revenue share to each contributing practice.
non_obvious_insight: Ranchers under-report to the state because reporting costs them money, but they do not hide problems from their vet because they need the vet's drugs and help. The vet's phone is the earliest sensor in the system, and vets cannot share client data but can share counts. Contrarian point: the absence of calls is also a signal, because call volume drops when producers hide problems during a quarantine.
first_30_days: Recruit 25 large-animal practices in Texas, Oklahoma, New Mexico, Kansas and Nebraska through state VMA lists and large-animal vet Facebook groups. Build the weekly tally as a plain SMS survey, with no software integration. Publish a free regional weekly newsletter to the vets as the hook. Backtest screwworm lead time against USDA confirmation dates and pitch 3 market-advisory or cattle analytics shops for a $1-2K per month paid pilot.

competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: SAVSNET / FAVSNET (University of Liverpool), Morrison Swine Health Monitoring Project (Univ. of Minnesota) and Swine Health Information Center (SHIC), Equine Disease Communication Center (US Equestrian), USDA APHIS / NAHLN and Texas Animal Health Commission (mandatory reporting). White space: Verdict basis: I found no commercial or non-commercial system that turns weekly counts from US large-animal (cattle) vet practices into a regional syndromic index sold to institutional buyers. I could not test that claim against Crunchbase, YC, TechCrunch or Product Hunt, so treat it as unconfirmed on the startup side.

What exists today:
- Academic systems, mostly in Europe (SAVSNET/FAVSNET in the UK).
- A 2025 scoping review of 126 animal syndromic systems: 67 percent were still proof-of-concept, only 20 percent were fully operational, and it noted that even established systems are vulnerable to loss of funding. Operational ones were mostly government run. This is a nearby-review finding, not proof that nobody is building this in the US. Source: https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pubmed&retmode=xml&id=40327964
- Free industry models such as MSHMP (swine) and the equine EDCC.
- Companion-animal practice data businesses (Animalytix, Vetsource).
- Government mandatory reporting, which now covers confirmed and suspected screwworm within 24 hours in Texas.

Unserved, specifically:
1. Pre-confirmation, syndromic, cattle-specific signals: abortion clusters, maggot wounds, sudden deaths and milk drops, at ZIP3 or county level, weekly. Government reporting only covers confirmed or suspected reportable disease.
2. A denominator and absence-of-calls signal that no current system produces.
3. A decision-grade product for private actors who face NWS movement restrictions and have no ground-level feed: sale barns, order buyers, feedlots, packers, insurers and animal health territory teams.

Structural risks that keep this a gap rather than open:
- Government and free alternatives (TAHC and USDA public case counts, EDCC-style free alerts) satisfy much of the need.
- Vets are legally obligated to report suspects to TAHC, so a private feed adds little for confirmed cases.
- Privacy and trade-implication concerns were the top barrier in an Australian stakeholder study (https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pubmed&retmode=xml&id=40037116).
- Selling vet-sourced early disease signals to commodity funds carries legal and ethics exposure (material non-public information, duty-to-report conflicts).

title: Ground-Truth Diligence for GPU-Backed Lenders
one_liner: Independent-engineer-style diligence and monthly monitoring on the part of a data center build that satellites cannot see: the last 90 days before ready-for-service.
customer: Private credit funds, banks and ABS investors lending against GPUs and neocloud contracts; insurers underwriting delay risk; AI labs and enterprises signing take-or-pay capacity who need to know if the promised RFS date is credible.
problem: GPU-backed loans and offtake contracts are priced on a ready-for-service date. Satellite vendors (SynMax and Industrial Info Resources now cover 2,600+ projects weekly) can show steel, cooling towers and generator yards, but they cannot see the failure zone: utility permission to energize, MV switchgear energization, Level 4/5 commissioning and IST results, liquid-cooling flush and pressure tests, fiber-plant acceptance, OEM startup-tech availability. Percent complete on pay applications is front-loaded and misleading. Meanwhile GPUs costing millions per rack sit idle and depreciate while interest accrues, and lenders are capping neocloud exposure. Traditional IEs are power-plant-oriented, slow and expensive.
solution: A 'Readiness Ladder' of about 40 binary, evidence-backed milestones (utility energization letter, gear serials and bills of lading, Cx level sign-offs, IST pass/fail counts, CDU flush logs, open-punch burn-down rate, OEM startup-tech calendar). Score each project and re-score monthly. Output a probability of RFS by date and covenant or draw-release triggers. Staff it with a bench of ex-data-center PMs and Cx leads who do desk review plus quick site visits. Sell as a 2-week second-opinion product first, then monthly monitoring, integrating vendor satellite feeds as an input rather than competing with them.
why_now: Neocloud credit risk is now the topic. Lenders are capping exposure, deals are stalling on credit risk, and GPU-debt structures (including vendor backstops) are proliferating. Analyses show roughly 40% of AI data center sites with possible delays and about half of 2026 capacity slipping, while operators publicly deny it. Satellite monitoring has commoditized the exterior, which makes the interior truth the scarce and valuable part.
revenue_model: $25K fixed-fee 2-week second opinions; $40K-120K full pre-close diligence; $8K-20K/month per facility monitoring; optional success-based fee for delay-risk insurance placement. Adjacent product: retained RFS-credibility scoring for AI labs choosing between capacity offers.
non_obvious_insight: Percent complete is the wrong metric. The last 5% of a data center can consume 25% of the calendar, and it is dominated by unbounded tasks: the commissioning punch-list burn-down rate and whether the OEM has a startup technician free that month predict RFS far better than construction progress. You can only read those signals if you have run an IST. Also, the RFS date on a marketing sheet is a sales number, not a schedule.
first_30_days: Recruit 6 retired or between-jobs Cx leads and PMs on 1099 contracts. Publish a free 'RFS credibility checklist' and a teardown of one publicly delayed project. Approach 5-10 private credit and infrastructure funds with data center or GPU-lending desks. Offer a fixed-fee $25K second opinion on one live deal, delivered in two weeks, and ask permission to reference the engagement anonymously.
